(c) The Court may enter a Writ of Repossession in the absence of the debtor if the debtor fails to 
appear at the hearing despite proper notice. 
 
The Writ of Repossession shall provide that: 
 
(1) 
The property which has been specified is to be seized by the authorized enforcement 
officers and turned over to the judgment creditor; and 
 
(2) 
The enforcement officers are authorized to use reasonable force to enforce the Writ 
of Repossession.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Remedies for Violation of this Chapter
text:
(a)Any creditor and any agents or employees of any creditor who are found by the Tribal Court 
to be in deliberate or willful violation of the provisions of this Chapter governing repossession 
may be sanctioned appropriately. The Court shall afford any creditor fair notice and an 
opportunity for hearing prior to the order of sanctions. 
 
(b) Any person who violates this Chapter and any creditor whose agents or employees violate 
this Chapter shall be deemed to have breached the peace of the Delaware Tribe of Indians and 
they shall be liable to any debtor for any actual damages caused by the deliberate or negligent 
failure to comply with the provisions of this Chapter. 
 
 

34 
Chapter 11 
Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Judgments
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Foreign Judgments – When Recognized
text:
(a) The Tribal Court shall not recognize or enforce any foreign judgment unless the proponent of 
the foreign judgment: 
 
(1) Complies with the procedure set forth in this Section; 
 
(2) Submits proof that the person against whom the foreign judgment has been rendered is 
subject to the jurisdiction of the Tribal Court; 
 
(3) Submits proof that the foreign judgment is based on valid subject matter and personal 
jurisdiction; 
 
(4) Submits proof that an attempt was made to enforce the judgment in the jurisdiction in 
which the foreign judgment was rendered and that such attempt was unsuccessful; or good cause 
is shown why an attempt at enforcement of the foreign judgment in that jurisdiction would be 
futile; and 
 
(5) Submits proof that the foreign judgment is final and that no appeal therefrom is 
allowed. 
 
(b) The Tribal Court shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment when to do so would 
require the Tribe to waive its immunity from suit except when the Tribe is to be served as a 
garnishee for the wages or property of a judgment debtor, in which case the requirements for 
garnishment that are set out in this Chapter shall be followed. 
 
(c) The Tribal Court need not recognize a foreign judgment if: 
 
(1) The defendant in the proceedings in the foreign court did not receive notice of said 
proceedings in sufficient time to allow him or her to defend; 
 
(2) The foreign judgment decree or order violated the Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968, 25 
U.S.C. § 1301 -1341, or any state or federal constitution; 
 
(3) The foreign judgment was obtained by fraud; 
 
(4) The foreign judgment would serve to violate any federal law, tribal law, custom or 
tradition of the Delaware Tribe of Indians; 
 
(5) The cause of action on which the judgment is based is contrary to the general welfare of 
the Tribe or its members; or 
 
(6) The government from which the foreign judgment is issued does not provide reciprocal 
full faith and credit or comity to the orders, decrees and judgments of the Tribal Court.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Procedure for Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Judgments
text:
(a) The proponent of a foreign judgment shall file in the Tribal Court: 
 
(1) a certified copy of the foreign judgment, identifying the date of its entry; 
 
(2) the record of any subsequent entries affecting the judgment, such as levies of execution 
and payments in partial satisfaction; 
 
(3) a motion requesting that the Tribal Court recognize and enforce the foreign judgment; 
and 
 
(4) submission of proof required by this Chapter. 
 

 
35 
(b) A properly filed foreign judgment shall be docketed and recorded in the Tribal Court in the 
same manner as other cases. 
 
(c) Upon proper filing of a foreign judgment with the Tribal Court, the Court shall issue a 
summons directing the defendant to appear on a date not more that sixty (60) days or less than 
fifteen (15) days from the date of service and respond to the motion requesting the Tribal Court 
to recognize and enforce the foreign judgment. Such summons shall be served on the defendant 
in a manner consistent with this Title. 
 
(d) Failure of the defendant to appear as directed by the summons or failure to respond to the 
motion requesting the Court to recognize and enforce the foreign judgment once personal 
jurisdiction over the defendant has been obtained shall not prevent the Court from ruling on the 
motion. 
 
(e) After reviewing all the relevant evidence concerning the foreign judgment the Court shall 
issue an order granting or denying the motion to recognize and enforce the foreign judgment if 
doing so would be consistent with the provisions of this Chapter. Such an order shall be a final 
judgment of the Tribal Court in favor of either the plaintiff or defendant to the foreign judgment 
and shall be enforceable as such.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Severability
text:
If any provision of this Chapter or its application to any person or circumstances is held invalid, 
the remainder of this Chapter, or the application to other persons or other circumstances shall 
remain in effect. 
 
 

36 
 
Chapter 12 
Civil Forfeiture Procedures
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Property Which May be Forfeited
text:
(a) The Tribal Court may order forfeiture of the following kinds of property located within its 
jurisdiction: 
 
(1) Property which is made contraband by Tribal law; 
 
(2) Property being used to violate or in violation of Tribal law; 
 
(3) Property otherwise subject to forfeiture by specific Tribal law. 
 
(b) If a specific Tribal law sets forth its own forfeiture proceedings they shall be controlling and 
the Court may rely on such additional provisions in this chapter as justice may require.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Nature of Forfeiture
text: Forfeiture proceedings shall be in the nature of a civil suit against the property to be forfeited.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Initiating A Forfeiture Proceeding
text:
In order to initiate a forfeiture proceeding, the Tribe shall file a Petition for Forfeiture in the 
Court and deliver a copy of the petition to all persons believed to have an ownership interest in 
the property at issue.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Order for Seizure of Property
text:
Any time after a Petition for Forfeiture is filed, if the Tribe demonstrates that there is probable 
cause to believe the property named is subject to forfeiture under Tribal law, the judge may issue 
an order which directs Tribal law enforcement officers to seize and hold the property pending 
resolution of the forfeiture suit.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Seizure of Property Before Petition is Filed
text:
(a) In the following circumstances the Tribe, through its law enforcement officers, may seize any 
property which is subject to forfeiture before a Petition for Forfeiture is filed or before an order 
of seizure has been obtained: 
 
(1) When a Tribal law or regulation allows immediate seizure; 
 
(2) When the property presents an urgent danger to persons, property, or wildlife within the 
Tribe’s jurisdiction; 
 
(3) When the Tribe has probable cause to believe that the property is subject to forfeiture 
and is likely to be removed from the Tribe’s jurisdiction if it is not seized immediately. 
 
(b) Whenever the Tribe seizes property before it has filed and served a Petition for Forfeiture, it 
must file and serve the petition no later than five (5) days after the seizure has taken place. At the 
time of filling or as soon after that as the judge can schedule a hearing, the Tribe shall request an 
order of seizure as provided in this Chapter.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Inventory of Property and Notice of Seizure
text:
37 
(a) The Tribal officer who seizes property pursuant to these provisions shall prepare a complete 
list to a notice which states the time and place of seizure, the name and address of the owner, if 
known, and the authority for seizure. 
 
(b) The officer shall promptly deliver a copy of the notice and list to the Court, to the owner of 
the property, and to the person in whose possession the property was found. If the owner of the 
property cannot be identified or located, the officer shall post the notice and list at the place 
where the property was found and at the Court in a location visible to the public.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Release of Property Pending Forfeiture Trial
text:
(a) Pending the forfeiture trial, a person who presents satisfactory proof that he or she owns the 
property which has been seized may gain possession of the property by posting a bond or cash 
deposit with the Tribe. The bond or deposit shall be in the amount equal to the market value of 
the property. The amount and form of the bond shall be subject to approval of the Tribal court. 
 
(b) The Court shall order the Bond or cash forfeited if it is shown by a preponderance of the 
evidence that the owner used the property in violation of Tribal law after posting the bond. If the 
Court ultimately rules in the Tribe’s favor on the Petition for Forfeiture the court shall order 
either the bond or the property itself forfeited.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Procedures and Burdens of Proof
text:
Procedures and burdens of proof in a forfeiture proceeding shall be the same as in any civil suit, 
except that in cases where the property owner does not post bond and regain possession of the 
property, trial of the principle issue in the case must be held no later than thirty (30) days after 
the petition for forfeiture is filed. The property owner may voluntarily waive this right to a 
speedy hearing.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Disposition of the Property
text:
If the Court rules in favor of the property owner, all property seized or bonds or cash deposited 
shall promptly be returned to the owner. If the Court rules in favor of the Tribe, and orders the 
property forfeited, the Court’s order shall transfer title to the property of the Delaware Tribe of 
Indians. The Tribe may then dispose of the property as it sees fit. 
 
 
 

38 
Chapter 13 
Contempt of Court
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Contempt - Generally
text:
The Tribal Court shall at all times have authority to utilize contempt powers upon persons who 
may disobey orders, act in a manner that is disorderly or insolent. The contempt process shall be 
classified in two categories: (1) Direct Contempt and (2) Indirect Contempt.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Direct Contempt
text:
(a) Direct contempts shall exist where the Court makes a finding an individual’s behavior is 
 
(1) disorderly or insolent; and 
 
(2) committed during the session of the court, and in its immediate view and presence; 
 
(b) Individuals found to be in direct contempt of Court may be sanctioned appropriately and in a 
manner reasonable to the incidents leading up to the contemptuous activity or may be 
incarcerated for a period of time, not to exceed six (6) months.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Indirect Contempt
text:
(a) Indirect Contempt of court shall consist of: 
 
(1) willful disobedience of any process or order lawfully issued or made by the court; or 
 
(2) resistance willfully offered by any person to the execution of a lawful order or process 
of a court. 
 
(b) Individuals found to be in indirect contempt of Court may be sanctioned appropriately and in 
a manner reasonable to the incident leading up to the contemptuous activity or may be 
incarcerated for a period of time, not to exceed six (6) months.
heading_path: Title 13 CIVIL PROCEDURE

heading: Criminal code not applicable to traffic laws. The provisions of Title III do not
text:
apply to those situations in which a person is detained by a Tribal Officer for any violation of Title V 
of the Reno-Sparks Law and Order Code, unless specifically provided for in Title V.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Criminal jurisdiction. 
 
(a) An Indian defendant is subject to prosecution in Tribal Court for any offense enumerated 
in Chapter 2 of this Title or another Tribal ordinance when the offense is committed either totally or 
partially within the exterior boundaries of the Colony. 
 

4 
 
 
(b) An offense is committed partially within the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony if either the 
conduct which is an element of the offense or the result which is an element occurs within the 
exterior boundaries of the Colony. 
 
(c) An offense based on an omission to perform a duty imposed by Tribal law is committed 
within the exterior boundaries of the Colony regardless of the location of the defendant at the time of 
the omission. 
 
(d) The Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and Evidence shall apply in Tribal Court in any 
areas of criminal procedure or evidence not covered or provided for in the code, or where provisions 
of this code are deemed incomplete or in need of further elaboration or clarification.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Rights of the defendant. 
 
(a) In all criminal proceedings, the defendant shall have the following rights: 
(1) to be released from custody pending trial or hearing upon payment of reasonable 
bail, unless the Tribal Court finds he is a serious risk to flee the jurisdiction of the Court or is a 
serious threat of harm to the community or members thereof, including himself; 
(2) to appear and defend in person, by privately obtained attorney, tribal advocate, 
tribal member, or other person lawfully admitted to practice under the provisions in this Code. Class 
A offenses, however, may be prosecuted without the presence of the defendant upon a showing that 
the defendant received actual notice of the proceedings at least five (5) days prior to the proceeding; 
(3) to be informed of the nature of the charges pending against him and to have a 
copy of those charges by the time of arraignment; 
(4) to confront and cross examine all prosecution or hostile witnesses; 
(5) to compel by subpoena the attendance of any witnesses necessary to defend 
against the charges and/or the production of any books, records, documents, or other items necessary 
to defend against the charges; 
(6) to have a speedy public trial by judge or jury, unless the right to speedy trial is 
waived by the defendant or his counsel on his behalf and with his consent. Subject to the provisions 
of Section 3-1-105.5 speedy trial is the right to be tried within 120 days of arraignment if out of 
custody or 70 days if incarcerated; 
(7) to appeal any final decision of the Tribal Court to a Tribal Court of Appeals; 
(8) to not be twice put in jeopardy by the Tribal Court for the same offense. Jeopardy 
attaches when the first witness is sworn; and 
(9) to remain silent and not be required to testify against himself; or have any 
inference drawn from exercising this right. 
 
(b) No interference may be drawn from a defendant's exercise not to testify.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Presence of defendant. 
 
(a) Unless otherwise provided herein, a defendant must be present at all stages of the 
proceedings, and if he fails to appear, the Tribal Court may issue a warrant for his arrest. 
 
(b) The Tribal Court in its discretion may allow the defendant to appear though counsel, 
except at stages where testimony is to be taken, or sentencing is to be pronounced. 
 
(c) Any defendant who is legally represented has the legal obligation to maintain sufficient 
contact with his legal representative to know when his appearance in Tribal Court is required, and 
notice to the defendant's representative is constructive notice imputed to the defendant.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Subsequent prosecutions. 
(a) A subsequent prosecution will not constitute double jeopardy when the previous 
prosecution was properly terminated under the following circumstances: 

7 
 
 
(1) the defendant consents to the termination or waives, by motion, an appeal upon a 
judgment of conviction or otherwise, the right to object to the termination of the prosecution; 
(2) the Tribal Court finds that a termination, other than by acquittal, is necessary 
because: 
(i) it is impossible to proceed with the trial in conformity with the law; 
(ii) there is a legal defect in the proceeding that would make any judgment 
entered upon a verdict reversible as a matter of law; 
(iii) prejudicial conduct in or outside the courtroom, makes it impossible to 
proceed with the trial without injustice to either the defendant or the Colony, 
(iv) the jury cannot agree upon a verdict; or 
(v) a false statement of a juror on voir dire prevents a fair trial; 
(3) the former prosecution occurred in a court which lacked jurisdiction over the 
defendant or the offense; 
(4) the subsequent prosecution was for an 'offense which was not completed when the 
former prosecution began; or 
(5) there was a transfer of jurisdiction to another authority. 
 
Part 2. Investigative Procedures
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Investigation of suspicious death. 
 
(a) Tribal law enforcement shall conduct an investigation whenever there is information 
that: 
(1) death was caused by other than natural causes; 
(2) death occurred under circumstances indicating the involvement of possible 
criminal conduct; or 
(3) no licensed physician or surgeon will sign a death certificate. 
 
(b) It shall be the duty of every person acquiring information pertaining to such a death to 
report the information to the Tribal police. 
 
(c) In a case where criminal conduct is suspected, the Tribal Chief of Police or someone 
designated by the Tribal Chief of Police shall notify a medical examiner and one or more law 
enforcement agencies having jurisdiction. The law enforcement agencies so notified shall have the 
responsibility to investigate the case. 
 
(d) The Tribal Chief of Police may, at his discretion, order an autopsy to be performed by a 
medical examiner. 
(1) A full record of the facts found shall be made by the medical examiner and copies 
provided to the coroner and Tribal prosecutor's office. 
(2) The right to conduct an autopsy shall include the right to retain such specimens as 
the medical examiner performing the autopsy deems necessary. 
(3) The Tribe shall pay any expenses incurred whenever an autopsy or investigation is 
initiated at the request of the Tribal Chief of Police.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Investigative subpoenas. 
 

8 
 
 
(a) Whenever the Tribal Prosecutor has the duty to investigate alleged unlawful activity, a 
judge may cause a subpoena to be issued commanding a specified person to appear before the Tribal 
Prosecutor, or a designated agent of the prosecutor, and give testimony and produce such books, 
records, papers, documents, and other objects as may be necessary and proper to the investigation. 
 
(b) No person subpoenaed under this provision is required to give testimony or produce any 
evidence, which may incriminate him, unless granted immunity. 
 
(c) An investigative subpoena may only be issued by a judge when supported by an affidavit 
of the prosecutor sufficient to show that the administration of justice requires the testimony or 
information being sought
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Relief from improper subpoena. A person aggrieved by a subpoena issued
text:
pursuant to this Part may, within a reasonable time, file a motion to dismiss the subpoena and, in the 
case of a subpoena duces tecum, to limit its scope. The motion must be granted if the subpoena was 
improperly issued or, in the case of a subpoena duces tecum, if it was overly broad in its scope.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Conduct of investigative hearing. 
 
(a) Before a Judge, the prosecutor may examine under oath all witnesses subpoenaed 
pursuant to this part. Testimony must be recorded. The witness has a right to have counsel present at 
all times. Failure to obey a subpoena served under this part, without just cause, is punishable by 
contempt of court. 
 
(b) Proceedings conducted under this part are closed proceedings, except to the extent that 
they supply probable cause for arresting or charging the defendant in a subsequent criminal action or 
are admissible in a later criminal trial. A person who divulges the contents of the Prosecutor's 
affidavit or the proceedings without legal privilege to do so is punishable for contempt of court. 
 
(c) All penalties for perjury or preparing, submitting, or offering false evidence apply to 
proceedings conducted under this section.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Self-incrimination — immunity. 
 
(a) No person subpoenaed to give testimony pursuant to this part may be required to make a 
statement or to produce evidence that may be personally incriminating. 
 
(b) The prosecutor may, with the approval of the judge who authorized the issuance of the 
subpoena, grant a person subpoenaed immunity from the use of any compelled testimony or 
evidence or any information directly or indirectly derived from the testimony or evidence against 
that person in a criminal prosecution. 
 
(c) Nothing in this part prohibits the Prosecutor from granting immunity from prosecution 
for or on account of any transaction, matter, or thing concerning which a witness is compelled to 
testify if the prosecutor determines, in the prosecutor's sole discretion, that the best interest of justice 
would be served by granting immunity. 

9 
 
 
 
(d) After being granted immunity, no person may be excused from testifying on the grounds 
that the testimony may be personally incriminating. Immunity may not extend to prosecution or 
punishment for false statements given pursuant to the subpoena. 
 
(e) Nothing in this section requires a witness to divulge the contents of privileged 
communication unless the privilege is waived as provided by law.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Authorization for Search and Seizure. A search of a person, object, or place may
text:
be made and evidence, contraband or persons may be seized in accordance with provisions of this 
Chapter when the search is made; 
 
(a) with the consent of the accused or any other person who, upon probable cause, is 
believed to be in lawful possession of the object or place to be searched by the law enforcement 
officer making the search; 
 
(b) in accordance with the authority set forth in a valid search warrant; or 
 
(c) in accordance with federally judicially recognized exceptions to the warrant requirement.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Scope of search after lawful arrest. When a lawful arrest is effected, a law
text:
enforcement officer may make a reasonable search of the person arrested and the area within such 
person's immediate presence, without a search warrant, for the purpose of: 
 
(a) protecting the officer from attack; 
 
(b) discovering and seizing the fruits of the crime; 
 
(c) discovering and seizing instruments, articles, or other property which may have been 
used in the commission of the offense, or which may constitute evidence of the offense, in order to 
prevent its destruction; or 
 
(d) preventing the person from escaping.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Search Warrants. 
 
(a) A "search warrant" is a court order: 
(1) in writing; 
(2) in the name of the Tribe; 
(3) signed by a judge of the Tribal Court; 
(4) particularly describing the property, place, or persons to be searched and the 
instruments, articles, or items to be seized; and 
(5) directed to a law enforcement officer commanding the officer to search for all 
named property and bring it before the judge. 

10 
 
 
(b) Every judge of the Tribal Court has the authority to issue warrants if probable cause 
exists for search and seizure of the premises and property of any person under the Tribal Court's 
jurisdiction.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Grounds for search warrant. 
 
(a) No search warrant shall be issued except upon a written or orally sworn statement of a 
law enforcement officer or Tribal Prosecutor, based upon reliable information and stating facts 
sufficient to support probable cause to believe that an offense has been committed, particularly 
describing the place, object or persons to be searched and/or seized. Probable cause must exist to 
indicate a search will discover: 
(1) stolen property, embezzled property, contraband or otherwise criminally 
possessed property; 
(2) property which has been or is being used to commit a criminal offense; or 
(3) property which constitutes evidence of the commission of a criminal offense. 
 
(b) When a warrant is requested based upon oral testimony, communicated by telephone or 
otherwise, a judge shall: 
(1) immediately place the requesting person(s) under oath; 
(2) record by voice recording device if available, or otherwise make a verbatim 
record, of the requesting person's statement and certify the accuracy of this record; 
(3) enter on an original warrant the grounds indicating probable cause exists to issue a 
warrant and the scope of the search warrant as requested or as modified; 
(4) sign the original warrant and enter on the face of the original warrant the exact 
time when the warrant was ordered to be issued; and 
(5) direct the requesting party to: 
(i) prepare a document identical to the original warrant to be known as a 
duplicate original warrant: 
(ii) sign the duplicate original warrant on behalf of the judge; and 
(iii) enter the exact time of execution on the face of the duplicate original 
warrant. 
 
(c) A judge may require the applicant to furnish further testimony or documentary evidence 
in support of the application of the warrant.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Execution of a search warrant. 
 
(a) Search warrants shall only be executed by law enforcement officers between the hours of 
6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m., unless the issuing judge otherwise authorizes the warrant to be served 
anytime day or night. 
 
(b) Before entering the premises named in the search warrant, the law enforcement officer 
shall give appropriate notice of his or her identity, authority and purpose to the person to be 
searched, or to the person in apparent control of the premises to be searched. 
 

11 
 
 
(c) Before undertaking any search or seizure pursuant to the warrant, the executing law 
enforcement officer shall read and give a copy of the original or duplicate original warrant to the 
person to be searched, or to the person in apparent control of the premises to be searched. If the 
premises are unoccupied or there is no one in apparent control, the law enforcement officer shall 
leave a copy of the warrant suitably affixed to the premises. 
 
(d) If the warrant is executed, a duplicate copy and a receipt for all articles taken shall be left 
with any person over the age of eighteen (18) at the place from which any items were seized. 
 
(e) Failure to give or leave a receipt of all items seized shall not render the seized property 
inadmissible at any subsequent trial. 
 
(f) Only reasonable and necessary force may be used to execute a search warrant. 
 
(g) The executing officer shall return the warrant to the Tribal Court within the time limit 
shown on the face of the warrant. A warrant is only effective within ten (10) days of the date of 
issuance excluding the date of issuance. Warrants not executed within such time limits shall be void.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: What may be seized with search warrant. A warrant may be issued under this
text:
section to search for and seize any: 
 
(a) evidence; 
 
(b) contraband; or 
 
(c) person for whose arrest there is probable cause, for whom there has been a warrant of 
arrest issued, or who is unlawfully restrained.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Scope of search pursuant to search warrant. 
 
(a) The scope of any search shall only include those areas specifically authorized by the 
warrant and is limited to the least restrictive means reasonably necessary to discover the person or 
property specified in the warrant. 
 
(b) Upon discovery of the person or property named in the warrant, the law enforcement 
officer shall take possession or custody of the person or property and search no further under the 
authority of the warrant. 
 
(c) If, in the course of an authorized search, the law enforcement officer discovers property 
not specified in the warrant and the officer has probable cause to believe the discovered property 
constitutes evidence of the commission of a criminal offense, or contraband, the officer may also 
take possession of that property.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Disposition of Property Seized. 
(a) A hearing may be requested before the Tribal Court within 10 working days of any 
seizure to determine the disposition of all property seized by law enforcement officers. 

12 
 
 
(b) Upon satisfactory proof of ownership, the property shall be delivered to the owner, 
unless such property is contraband or is to be used as evidence in a pending case. 
 
(c) Non-contraband property taken as evidence shall be returned to the owner after final 
judgment has been rendered. 
 
(d) Non-contraband property may be returned to the owner prior to final judgment upon 
application to and at the discretion of the Tribal Court. 
 
(e) Property confiscated as contraband or taken as evidence and of unknown ownership and 
unclaimed for a period of six months shall become the property of the Colony and may be: 
(1) destroyed; 
(2) sold at public auction; 
(3) retained for the benefit of the Colony; 
(4) lawfully disposed of as ordered by the Tribal Court; or 
(5) otherwise disposed of in accordance with Colony Law.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Investigative Stops. 
 
(a) A law enforcement officer may stop and make a limited inquiry of any person when the 
observed circumstances give the officer reasonable articulated suspicion to suspect that the person 
has committed, is committing, or is about to commit a recognized offense. 
 
(b) A law enforcement officer may stop any person found near the scene of an offense and 
make a limited inquiry pertaining to the immediate circumstances that aroused the officer's 
suspicion, when the officer has probable cause: 
(1) to suspect the person has information which will materially aid in the 
investigation of the offense; and 
(2) a need to obtain or verify the person's identity or an account of the offense. 
 
(c) A law enforcement officer who has lawfully stopped a person under this part may: 
(1) frisk or pat search the person and take other reasonable steps necessary for 
protecting herself or himself, or any other persons present; 
(2) take possession of any object discovered during the course of the frisk if there is 
reasonable cause to believe the object is criminally possessed property or a deadly weapon; and 
(3) demand the name and present address of the person. 
 
(d) Any person lawfully stopped by a law enforcement officer must be notified as soon as 
possible that: 
(1) the person making the stop is a law enforcement officer; 
(2) the stop is not an arrest but rather a temporary detention for investigation; 
(3) upon completion of the investigation, the person will be released if not arrested. 
 
(e) After the authorized purpose of the stop has been accomplished or a reasonable time has 
elapsed to complete such temporary detention, whichever occurs first, the law enforcement officer 
shall either allow the person to leave, or place the person under arrest. 

13
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Roadblocks. 
 
(a) Law enforcement officers may establish a temporary roadblock upon any roadway to 
apprehend a person suspected of committing a criminal offense. 
 
(b) Unless exigent circumstances exist justifying a departure from the requirements listed 
below, law enforcement officers shall make every effort to abide by the following procedures at the 
earliest possible time: 
(1) the temporary roadblock must be visible at a distance of not less than 100 yards in 
either direction; 
(2) an authorized emergency vehicle must be clearly marked as such and with its 
warning lights in operation, must be placed so as to be clearly visible to traffic affected by the 
roadblock at a distance of not less that 100 yards; 
(3) at least one flashing or intermittent light must be placed at the side of the 
roadway, clearly visible to the oncoming traffic at a distance of not less than 100 yards; and 
(4) at the point of the temporary roadblock, cones, reflectors, burning flares or similar 
devised must be in place to identify the point of the roadblock and direct, if necessary, the path to be 
followed by a vehicle approaching the roadblock; 
(5) warning signs which will attract an oncoming driver's attention must be places at 
least 200 yards prior to the roadblock indicating that all vehicles should be prepared to stop; and 
(6) at a point located not less than 200 yards, but not more than 400 yards, from the 
point of the temporary roadblock, cones, reflectors, burning flares or similar devices must be placed 
on both shoulders of the roadway and near the centerline of the roadway to warn traffic that a 
condition hazardous to traffic exists in the immediate vicinity. 
 
Part 3. Commencing Criminal Prosecution
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Citation. Prosecution for all Class A offenses may be initiated by citation issued
text:
by a law enforcement officer upon probable cause where the officer has attested to the truth of the 
allegations contained in the citation under oath.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Complaint. 
 
(a) All criminal prosecutions for Class B and C offenses shall be initiated by complaint. 
 
(b) The complaint is a written statement of the essential facts charging that a named 
individual has committed a particular criminal offense. 
 
(c) Application for leave to file a complaint shall be made by a Tribal Prosecutor to a judge. 
The application shall be by affidavit which is based on probable cause that the crime charged 
happened and that the defendant(s) committed the crime charged. When leave to file a complaint has 
been granted, a warrant or summons may issue for the defendant's arrest or appearance. The Tribal 
Prosecutor shall file the complaint within 30 days after leave of court is granted. 
 
(d) The complaint shall contain: 
 

14 
 
 
(1) The name of the person accused, if known, or a description sufficient to identify 
the person accused of committing the alleged offense; 
(2) The general location where the alleged offense was committed; 
(3) The name and code citation of the alleged offense; 
(4) A short, concise statement of the specific acts or omissions to act constituting an 
offense; 
(5) The person, if any, against whom the alleged offense was committed, if known, 
except in the case of a sexual offense or an offense involving a minor; 
(6) The date and approximate time of the commission of the alleged offense, if 
known; and 
(7) The signature of a Tribal Prosecutor. 
 
(e) No minor omission from or error in the form of the complaint shall be grounds for 
dismissal unless the defendant is shown to be significantly prejudiced by the omission or error. 
 
(f) A specific Class of an offense need not be included in the complaint. If a factual 
allegation is contained in the complaint which will supply the information needed to determine the 
degree of the offense, the Judge may use that information to determine bail. If no factual allegation 
is made, the offense shall be considered the least degree possible under the offense charged for the 
purposes of setting bail. 
 
(g) The judge shall examine the Complaint and Affidavit to: 
(1) Ascertain the validity of the complaint; 
(2) Determine whether probable cause exists to believe that the defendant has 
committed the crime alleged; and 
(3) Decide whether an arrest warrant or a summons should issue. 
 
(h) The judge may hold a preliminary hearing to determine whether probable cause exists to 
believe that the defendant has committed the crime charged.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Amending the complaint. 
 
(a) A complaint may be amended in matters of substance at any time prior to arraignment 
without leave of the Tribal Court. 
 
(b) A complaint may be amended in matters of substance at any time not less than 5 days 
before trial with leave of the Tribal Court. 
 
(c) When the prosecution seeks leave to amend a complaint as to a matter of substance, the 
prosecutor shall file: 
(1) A motion for leave to amend stating the nature of the proposed amendment; 
(2) A copy of the proposed complaint, as amended; and 
(3) An affidavit setting forth facts and circumstances sufficient to show probable 
cause exists to justify the amended complaint. 
 

15 
 
 
(d) If the motion is timely filed and the amended complaint is supported by probable cause, 
the court shall grant leave to amend. 
 
(e) The defendant shall be arraigned on the amended complaint without unreasonable 
delay. 
 
(f) The defendant shall be given a reasonable period of time to prepare for trial on the 
amended complaint. 
 
(g) The Tribal Court may permit a complaint to be amended as to form at any time before a 
verdict or a finding if no additional or different offense is charged and if the substantial rights of the 
defendant are not prejudiced. 
 
(h) No charge may be dismissed because of a formal defect which does not tend to prejudice 
any substantial right of the defendant.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Joinder and severance of offenses and defendants. 
 
(a) Two or more offenses may be charged in the same complaint in separate counts, or 
alternatively, if the offenses charged are of the same or similar character and are based on the same 
transactions connected together or constituting parts of a common scheme or plan. Allegations made 
in one count may be incorporated by reference in another count. 
 
(b) The Tribal Court may order that different offenses or counts set forth in the complaint be 
tried separately or consolidated. 
 
(c) The prosecution is not required to elect between the different offenses or counts set forth 
in the complaint and the defendant may be convicted of any number of the offenses charged, except 
as provided in Section 3-1-306. Each offense of which the defendant is convicted must be stated in 
the verdict or the finding of the Tribal Court.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Discharge of co-defendant. 
 
(a) When two or more persons are charged with offenses arising from the same incident, the 
Tribal Court may, at any time prior to the defendant presenting their cases and upon application of 
the prosecutor, dismiss the charges against any defendant so that the defendant may be a witness for 
the prosecution. 
 
(b) When two or more persons are included in the same complaint and the Tribal Court 
determines that there is insufficient evidence to prosecute one of the named defendants, the Tribal 
Court must discharge that defendant before the evidence is closed so that the discharged defendant 
may be a witness for the co-defendant.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Multiple charges from the same transaction. 
(a) When the same transaction may establish the commission of more than one offense, a 
person charged with the conduct may be prosecuted for each offense. 

16 
 
 
(b) A person may not, however, be convicted of more than one offense if: 
(1) One offense is included in the other; 
(2) One offense consists only of a conspiracy or other form of preparation to commit 
the other; 
(3) Inconsistent findings of fact are required to establish the commission of the 
offenses; 
(4) The offenses differ only in that one is defined to prohibit a specific instance of 
conduct; or 
(5) The offense is defined to prohibit a continuing course of conduct, and the 
defendant's course of conduct was interrupted, unless the law provides that the specific periods of 
the conduct constitute separate offenses. 
 
Part 4. Arrest and Related Procedures
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Method of arrest. 
 
(a) An arrest is made by actually restraining the person to be arrested or by that person 
voluntarily submitting to the custody of the person making the arrest. 
 
(b) All necessary and reasonable force may be used in making an arrest, but the person 
arrested shall not be subject to any greater restraint than is necessary to hold or detain the person. 
 
(c) All necessary and reasonable force may be used to effect an entry into any building or 
property or part thereof to make an authorized arrest.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Arrest by law enforcement officer. 
 
(a) A law enforcement officer may arrest a person anywhere within the exterior boundaries of 
the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony under the following circumstances: 
(1) the officer possesses or has reasonable belief that a signed arrest warrant has been 
issued by a judge against the person; 
(2) when the person has committed an offense in the officer's presence; 
(3) the officer has probable cause, as reflected by stated and provable facts, to believe 
the person to be arrested has committed an offense and exigent circumstances require an immediate 
warrantless arrest in order to prevent the person from: 
(i) fleeing the jurisdiction or concealing himself to avoid arrest; 
(ii) destroying or concealing evidence of the commission of an offense; 
(iii) injuring another person; or 
(iv) damaging property belonging to another. 
 
(b) When an arrest is made without an arrest warrant, the arresting officer must inform the 
person to be arrested, as soon as practicable, of his or her authority to make the arrest and the 
reasons for making the arrest. 
 

17 
 
 
(c) Whenever a law enforcement officer has probable cause to arrest a person without a 
warrant, the officer may instead issue a citation requiring the person to appear before a Tribal judge. 
The citation shall: 
(1) be in writing; 
(2) state the name of the person and the person's address, if known; 
(3) set forth the nature of the offense and cite the Law and Order Code Section; 
(4) direct the person to appear in Tribal Court at a specific date and time, but within 
fourteen (14) working days from the date of service, to enter a plea to the charge; and 
(5) be signed by the issuing officer.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure
Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure
Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Warrants issued after a summons. Upon information indicating the person is
text:
unlikely to appear by summons, or upon failure of the person summoned to appear, the Tribal Judge 
shall issue a warrant of arrest.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Arresting law enforcement officer's liability. No law enforcement officer shall
text:
be held civilly or criminally liable for arresting any person under the Tribal Court's jurisdiction 
where there is probable cause to believe the person has violated a Tribal law, tribal, federal or 
recognized state or local law, providing that the officer acts in good faith and without malice.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Notification of rights prior to interrogations. 
 
(a) Prior to questioning any person in official custody, the law enforcement officer must 
inform the person in clear and unequivocal terms of the following rights: 
(1) that the person has the right to remain silent; 
(2) that anything said by him can and will be used against the person in any 
subsequent court proceeding; 
(3) that the person has the right to obtain legal counsel or representation at her or his 
own expense prior to answering any questions; and 
(4) that if at any point during questioning the person indicates that he wishes to 
remain silent or obtain legal counsel at his own expense, the questioning will cease. 
 
(b) Any statement obtained in violation of these rights may not be admitted into evidence. 
 
(c) The fact that a person chooses to remain silent cannot be used against him in any 
subsequent court proceeding.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Extradition. 
 
(a) If a Tribal law enforcement officer arrests any individual based on a warrant issued by 
another jurisdiction which has been filed with the Tribal Court or upon reasonable belief that a 
warrant has been issued by a jurisdiction other that the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony, he shall be 
entitled to a hearing before the Tribal Court on the following issues: 
(1) whether such warrant exists; and 
(2) whether the individual arrested is the named person on the warrant; and 
(3) whether the court issuing such warrant had jurisdiction to issue the warrant; 
and 
(4) whether the arrest made by Tribal law enforcement was lawful. 
 
(b) After being fully informed of his rights, the defendant may, in writing, waive the right to 
a hearing. If not waived, the hearing shall be held within two days of the arrest, and the defendant 
shall be entitled to bail at the sum set in the warrant. 
 

19 
 
 
(c) If at the hearing the Court does not find these factors to be established by the Tribal 
Prosecutor by clear and convincing proof, it shall order the defendant immediately released. If at the 
hearing the Court finds these factors to be established by the Tribal Prosecutor by clear and 
convincing proof, it shall order the defendant held for a reasonable time not to exceed ten days, after 
any Reno-Sparks Indian Colony sentence be served, for the other jurisdiction to retrieve the 
defendant. After the hearing the defendant may be admitted to bail in an amount to be set by the 
Tribal Court, on the condition that he surrender himself at a specified time, and on such additional 
restrictions as the Court may deem appropriate. If such other jurisdiction does not retrieve the 
defendant within that time, the defendant shall be released. 
 
(d) Nothing in this section shall be considered to limit or restrict an individual's right to seek 
a writ of habeas corpus. 
 
Part 5. Initial Appearance
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Initial appearance. 
 
(a) A person arrested, whether with or without a warrant, must be taken before a judge of the 
Tribal Court for an initial appearance within 48 hours following the arrest, excluding weekends and 
holidays. 
 
(b) A person not arrested shall appear for initial appearance at the time and place designated 
in the citation or summons.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure
Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Right to counsel. 
 
(a) During the initial appearance before the court, every defendant must be informed of the 
right to have counsel, and must be asked if the aid of counsel is desired. 

20 
 
 
(b) If the defendant desires counsel but does not presently have counsel, the Tribal Court 
may grant the defendant reasonable time to obtain counsel and reappear before the Tribal Court for 
arraignment. 
 
(c) The defendant may exercise his right of self-representation. 
 
(d) A defendant may waive the right to counsel when the court ascertains that the waiver is 
made knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently in writing. 
 
Part 6. Bail
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Release prior to criminal proceedings. 
 
(a) Any person charged with any offense may be released on bail before conviction and shall 
be released from custody upon the posting of bail and/or upon other such reasonable and least 
restrictive conditions that ensure the appearance of the defendant at court proceedings and protect 
the safety of the community or of any person. 
 
(b) Any person in custody, if otherwise eligible for bail, may be released on his personal 
recognizance subject to such conditions as the court may reasonably prescribe to assure his 
appearance when required.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Reasonable bail. 
 
(a) In all cases, the amount set for bail must be reasonable. Reasonable bail reflects an 
amount which is: 
(1) sufficient to ensure the presence of the defendant in any pending criminal 
proceeding; 
(2) sufficient to assure compliance with the conditions set forth in a bail or release 
order; and 
(3) not oppressive.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Bail schedule. 
 
(a) The Chief Judge of the Tribal Court may, in his or her discretion, establish and post a 
schedule of bail for Class A, B and C offenses. 
 
(b) The Chief Judge shall review and if necessary, replace any existing bail schedule with a 
revised bail schedule by January 31 of each year. 
 
(c) Bail must be specifically set by a judge for any offenses not listed on the posted bail 
schedule.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Conditions of release. 

21 
 
 
(a) The Court may impose any condition that will reasonably ensure the appearance of the 
defendant as required or that will ensure the safety of any person or the community, including, but 
not limited to the following conditions: 
(1) the defendant shall remain in the custody of a designated person who agrees to 
supervise the defendant and report any violation of a release condition to the court, if the designated 
person is reasonably able to assure the court that the defendant will appear as required and will not 
pose a danger to the safety of any person or the community; 
(2) the defendant shall obey all laws and may not commit an offense during the 
period of release; 
(3) the defendant shall maintain employment, or, if unemployed, actively seek 
employment; 
(4) the defendant shall abide by specified restrictions of the defendant's personal 
associations, place of abode, and travel; 
(5) the defendant shall avoid all contact with an alleged victim of the crime and any 
potential witness who may testify concerning the offense; 
(6) the defendant shall comply with a specified curfew; 
(7) the defendant may not possess a firearm, destructive device, or other dangerous 
weapon; 
(8) the defendant may not use or possess alcohol, or any dangerous drag or other 
controlled substance without a legal prescription; 
(9) the defendant shall report on a regular basis to a designated agency or individual, 
or both; 
(10) the defendant shall furnish bail; or 
(11) the defendant shall return to custody for specified hours following release from 
employment, schooling or other approved purposes. 
 
(b) The Court shall subject the defendant to the least restrictive condition or combination of 
conditions that will ensure the defendant's appearance and provide for protection of any person or 
the community. At any time, the court may, upon a reasonable basis, amend the order to impose 
additional or different conditions of release upon its own motion or upon the motion of either party.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure
Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Release agreements. 
 
(a) If a defendant is released from custody pending a criminal proceeding, the conditions of 
release shall be set forth in an agreement signed by the defendant or placed on record as the needs 
dictate. 
 
(b) A release agreement shall specifically state all restrictions placed on the defendant, 
including that the defendant is to: 
(1) appear to answer the charges in the Tribal Court on a day certain and thereafter as 
ordered by the Tribal Judge until discharged or released by final order of the Tribal Court; 
(2) submit to all orders and process of the Tribal Court; 
(3) remain within the exterior boundaries of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony, unless 
given leave by the Tribal Court to depart from the Colony; and 
(4) comply with such other conditions of release as the Tribal Court may deem 
appropriate.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Changing bail or conditions of release. 
 
(a) Upon application by the Colony or the defendant, the Tribal Judge may increase or reduce 
the amount of bail, alter the conditions contained in a release agreement, or revoke the bail. If the 
amount of bail is reduced after it has been posted, the court shall return any amounts necessary to 
reflect the proper bail amount. 
 
(b) Reasonable notice of such application must be given to the opposing parties or their 
representatives. Such notice shall be given by personal service, by mail or by such means as are 
reasonably calculated to give all involved parties notice of possible changes in the release agreement 
or bail, and the date of the hearing regarding this matter.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Release of bail. When all conditions of release have been satisfactorily performed
text:
and the defendant has been discharged from any obligations imposed by the Tribal Court, the court 
shall return any security posted by the defendant to satisfy bail requirements.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Violation of conditions of release. 
 
(a) If a defendant violates a condition of release, including failure to appear, the prosecutor 
may make a motion to the court for revocation of the order of release. The Tribal Court may issue a 
warrant for the arrest of a defendant charged with violating a condition of release and declare the 
bail to be revoked. Upon arrest, the defendant must be brought before the Tribal Court without 
unnecessary delay and the Tribal Court shall conduct a hearing and redetermine bail. Upon finding 

23 
 
 
probable cause that the defendant has violated a tribal, state, or federal law, or upon finding a 
violation of any other release condition by clear and convincing evidence, the Tribal Court may: 
(1) reinstate the original release order on the same conditions and amount of bail; or 
(2) revoke the original bail, increase the amount of the bail, and/or modify the 
conditions of release. 
 
(b) This section provides the exclusive remedy for a violation of a release order. A defendant 
may not be charged with contempt or found in contempt for violation of a release order. 
 
(c) Neither a cash bond, nor a commercial bond, may be forfeited for violation of release 
conditions, except for failing to appear for court proceedings without a lawful excuse.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Forfeiture order. 
 
(a) Notice of an order of forfeiture must be mailed to the defendant and the defendant's 
sureties at their last known address within 10 working days of the date of the forfeiture order. 
 
(b) If within 30 days of the forfeiture order, the defendant, or the defendant's surety, appears 
and presents evidence justifying the defendant's failure to appear or otherwise meet the conditions 
found in the release order, the Tribal Court may direct the forfeiture of the bail to be discharged 
upon such terms as are just. 
 
(c) If the forfeiture order is not. discharged, the Tribal Court shall proceed with the forfeiture 
of bail as follows: 
(1) If money has been posted as bail, the court shall pay the money to the Tribal 
Treasurer; or 
(2) If other property is posted as a condition of release, the property must be sold in 
the same manner as property sold in civil actions. The proceeds of the sale must be used to satisfy all 
court costs and prior encumbrances, if any, and from the balance, a sufficient sum to satisfy the 
forfeiture must be paid to the Tribal Treasurer. 
 
Part 7. Arraignment
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Joint defendants. 
 
(a) Defendants who are jointly charged may be arraigned separately or together in the 
discretion of the Court.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Arraignment procedure. 
 
(a) A defendant shall be arraigned in open Tribal Court whenever a complaint or citation has 
been filed by the Tribal Prosecutor. For purposes of this subsection, an arraignment that is conducted 
by the use of two-way electronic audio-video communication, allowing all of the participants to be 
observed and heard in the courtroom by all present, is considered to be an arraignment in open court. 
 

24 
 
 
(b) The Tribal Court may arraign the defendant at the initial appearance without the presence 
of counsel or an advocate, if the defendant waives his right to counsel. 
 
(c) Arraignment consists of supplying a copy of the complaint to the defendant, reading the 
complaint, unless the defendant has waived the reading, and calling on the defendant to plead to the 
charge(s). 
 
(d) Prior to accepting any plea at the time of arraignment, the judge must: 
(1) verify that the defendant's true name appears on the complaint. If the defendant's 
true name is different than the name used on the complaint, the Tribal Court shall order the 
complaint amended to reflect the correct name; and 
(2) determine whether the defendant has a mental disorder that would prevent the 
defendant from understanding the charges, the penalties, or the effects of a plea, and if the 
determination is that defendant has a mental disorder, the arraignment may be continued until the 
defendant is able to proceed.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Plea alternatives at arraignment. 
 
(a) The defendant shall enter a plea of guilty, not guilty, or if the judge agrees, no contest, to 
all charges contained in the complaint. A plea of "no contest" may be accepted by a judge only after 
due consideration of the views of the parties and interests of the Colony in the effective 
administration of justice. 
 
(b) A defendant pleading not guilty must inform the judge within 10 days following 
arraignment if a jury trial is being requested. 
 
(c) If the defendant refuses to plead to the charges, the judge will enter a plea of not guilty 
on behalf of the defendant. Once a plea of not guilty is on the record, the judge shall order the matter 
scheduled for trial. 
 
(d) If the defendant voluntarily enters a plea of guilty or "no contest," the Judge shall make 
determinations as required in Section 34-802 prior to accepting the guilty or "no contest" plea. 
 
(e) After a judge has accepted a plea of guilty or "no contest", the judge may impose a 
sentence at that time or schedule a sentencing hearing in order to allow sufficient time for the 
involved parties to obtain any information deemed necessary for the imposition of a just sentence. 
 
(f) Prior to the imposition of any sentence, the Judge shall allow the defendant an 
opportunity to inform the judge of any extenuating or mitigating circumstances which might affect 
the severity of the pending sentence.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Plea agreement negotiations. 
 
(a) A prosecutor and counsel for the defendant, or the defendant when acting pro se, may 
engage in discussions with a view toward reaching an agreement that, upon the entering of a plea of 
guilty to a charged offense or to a lesser or related offense, the prosecutor will do one of the 
following: 
(1) move for dismissal of other charges; and/or 
(2) make a recommendation, or agree not to oppose the defendant's request, for a 
particular sentence, with the understanding that the recommendation or request may not be binding 
on the court. 
 
(b) A plea bargain agreement may be entered into any time prior to a verdict or finding of 
guilt by judge or jury.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Court procedure for accepting guilty plea. 
 
(a) If a plea agreement has been reached by the parties, the Tribal Court shall, on the record, 
require a disclosure of the agreement in open court at the time the plea is offered. 
 
(b) The court may not accept a plea of guilty or "no contest" at any time without first 
determining the following: 
(1) that the plea is voluntary and not the result of force or threats, or of promises apart 
from a plea agreement. The Tribal Court shall also inquire as to whether the defendant's willingness 
to plead guilty results from prior discussions between the prosecutor and the defendant or the 
defendant's attorney; 
(2) that the defendant understands the following: 
(i) the nature of the charge for which the plea is offered, 
(ii) any mandatory minimum penalty and the maximum penalty 
(iii) that restitution may be applicable; 
(iv) that the defendant will be giving up his right to a trial; and 
(v) that if the defendant pleads guilty in fulfillment of a plea agreement, the 
Court is not required to accept the terms of the agreement and that the defendant may not be entitled 
to withdraw the plea if the agreement is not accepted; 
 
(3) that the defendant is not under the influence of alcohol or drugs or has a mental 
disorder which would prevent the defendant from understanding the plea agreement or voluntarily 
agreeing to the plea agreement; and 
(4) that, in charges for which imprisonment is a possible penalty, there is factual basis 
for such plea. 
 
(c) With the approval of the Court and the consent of the Tribal Prosecutor, a defendant may 
enter a plea of guilty or "no contest," reserving the right, on appeal, from the judgment, to review the 
adverse determination of any specified pretrial motion. If the defendant prevails on appeal, the 
defendant must be allowed to withdraw the plea. 

26
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Telephonic change of plea. In exceptional circumstances and at its discretion, the
text:
Tribal Court may accept a defendant's change of plea through a recorded telephonic proceeding. 
 
Part 9. Pretrial Motions and Discovery
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Pretrial defenses and objections. 
 
(a) Except for good cause shown, any defense, objection, or request which is capable of 
determination without a trial on the general issues must be raised before trial by motion to dismiss or 
for other appropriate relief. All motions must be in writing and must be supported by a statement of 
the relevant facts upon which the motion is being made unless otherwise directed by the judge. 
 
(b) Failure of a party to raise defenses or objections or to make requests that must be made 
prior to trial, except lack of jurisdiction or the failure of a complaint to state an offense which may 
be noticed by the Tribal Court at any time during the pendency of a proceeding, constitutes a waiver 
of the defense, objection, or request. The Court, for good cause shown, may grant relief fi-Om any 
waiver provided in this section. 
 
(c) Motions in Limine should be made at least 5 days before trial, unless good cause is 
shown.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Suppression of evidence. 
 
(a) A defendant aggrieved by an unlawful search and seizure may move to suppress as 
evidence anything obtained by the unlawful search and seizure. The motion must be filed at least 10 
days before trial, unless good cause is shown for waiving this time restriction. 
 
(b) The motion must specify the evidence sought to be suppressed and the grounds upon 
which the motion is based. 
 
(c) When the motion to suppress challenges the admissibility of evidence obtained without a 
warrant, the prosecution has the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the 
search and seizure were valid. 
 
(d) If the motion is granted, the evidence is not admissible at trial.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Motion to suppress confession or admission. 
 
(a) A defendant may move to suppress as evidence any confession or admission given by 
him on the ground that it was not voluntary or that was otherwise obtained in violation of his rights. 
 
(b) The motion must be filed at least 10 days before trial, unless good cause is shown for 
waiving this time restriction. 
 
(c) If the allegations of the motion state facts which, if true, show the confession or 
admission was not voluntarily made or was otherwise obtained in violation of the defendant's rights, 

27 
 
 
the Tribal Court shall conduct a hearing on the merits of the motion. The prosecution must prove by 
a preponderance of the evidence that the confession or admission was not obtained in violation of the 
defendant's rights. 
 
(d) The issue of admissibility of the confession or admission may not be submitted to the 
jury. If the confession or admission is determined to be admissible, the circumstances surrounding 
the making of the confession or admission may be submitted to the jury as bearing upon the 
credibility or the weight to be given to the confession or admission. 
 
(e) If the motion to suppress is granted, the confession or admission may not be admitted 
into evidence by the prosecution at the time of trial.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Disclosure by prosecution. 
 
(a) At the time of the initial appearance, the prosecutor shall disclose to the defendant the 
name of the person, if any, against whom the offense was committed if not disclosed in the 
complaint. 
 
(b) At the arraignment or as soon thereafter as practicable the defendant may request notice 
of all evidence the prosecutor intends to use in the prosecution case-in-chief at trial. 
 
(c) Upon defendant's request, any of the following information or evidence which is within 
the possession, custody, or control of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony is subject to disclosure and 
production and may be copied or photographed, as appropriate for the item, by the defendant: 
(1) any relevant written or recorded statement made by the defendant while in the 
custody of the Tribal Police and of any person who will be tried with the defendant; 
(2) the names, addresses, and statements of all persons whom the prosecutor may call 
as witnesses in the case in chief. 
(3) the defendant's prior criminal record, if any; 
(4) any books, papers, documents, photographs, tangible objects, drawings of 
buildings or places, or other physical or demonstrative evidence which is intended for use by the 
prosecution at trial; 
(5) any written reports of or statements of experts who have personally examined the 
defendant or any evidence in the particular case, together with results of physical examinations, 
scientific tests or experiments, or comparisons; and 
(6) all material or information that tends to mitigate or negate the defendant's guilt as 
to the offense charged or that would tend to reduce the defendant's potential sentence. 
 
(d) At the same time, the prosecutor shall inform the defendant of, and make available to the 
defendant for examination and reproduction, any written or recorded material or information within 
the prosecutor's control regarding: 
(1) whether there has been any electronic surveillance of any conversation to which 
the defendant was a party; 
(2) whether an investigative subpoena has been executed in connection with the case; 
and 
(3) whether the case has involved an informant and, if so, the informant’s identity. 

28 
 
 
 
(e) Attorney work product of the Tribal Prosecutor's Office is not subject to disclosure and 
production. 
 
(f) The Prosecutor shall provide written notice of any evidence of other crimes, wrongs, or 
acts, that it intends to offer under Rule 404(b) of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony Rules of Evidence, 
at least two weeks prior to the close of discovery. The notice shall describe the evidence in sufficient 
detail to inform the defendant of the date, time, place and witnesses to the alleged incidents, and 
shall also state the purpose for which such evidence shall be offered. 
 
(g) The obligations imposed by this section are continuing.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Disclosure by defendant. 
 
(a) At any time after the filing of a complaint, the defendant, in connection with the particular 
offense charged, shall upon written request of the Tribal Prosecutor and approval by the Court: 
(1) appear in a lineup; 
(2) speak for identification by witnesses; 
(3) be fingerprinted, palm printed, footprinted, or voice taped; 
(4) pose for photographs not involving reenactment of an event; 
(5) try on clothing; 
(6) provide handwriting samples; 
(7) permit the taking of samples of the defendant's hair, blood, saliva, or urine or 
other specified materials that involved no unreasonable bodily intrusions; and 
(8) submit to a reasonable physical or medical examination where the examination 
does not involve psychological or psychiatric evaluation; 
 
(b) Except as provided in subsection (d), not later than the close of discovery upon request of 
the prosecution or at another time as the Tribal Court for good cause may permit, the defendant or 
defendant's counsel shall make available to the prosecutor for testing, examination, or reproduction: 
(1) the names, addresses, and statements of all persons, other than the defendant, 
whom the defendant may call as witnesses in the defense case in chief; 
(2) the names and addresses of experts whom the defendant may call at trial, together 
with the results of their physical examinations, scientific tests, experiments, or comparisons, 
including all written reports and statements made by these experts in connection with the particular 
case; and 
(3) all papers, documents, photographs, and other tangible objects that the defendant 
may use at trial. 
 
(c) At the close of discovery as set forth in the pretrial order, or at a later time as the Court 
shall permit, the defendant shall provide the prosecutor with a written notice of the defendant's 
intention to introduce evidence at trial of good character or any affirmative defenses. 
 
(d) The notice must specify for each defense the names and addresses of the persons, other 
than the defendant, whom the defendant may call as witnesses in support of the defense, together 
with all written reports or statements made by them, including all reports and statements concerning 

29 
 
 
the results of physical examinations, scientific tests, experiments, or comparisons, except that the 
defendant need not include a privileged report or statement unless the defendant intends to use the 
privileged report or statement, or the witness who made it, at trial. 
 
(e) Attorney work product by defense counsel is not subject to disclosure or production. 
 
(f) The obligations imposed by this section are continuing.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Severance. 
 
(a) A defendant may file with the Tribal Court a written motion requesting a severance of 
defendants or charges. Such motion shall be filed at least ten (10) days prior to trial unless otherwise 
directed by the Tribal Judge. 
 
(b) If it appears that the defendant or the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony is prejudiced either by a 
joinder or related prosecutions, or defendants in a single charge, or by joinder of separate charges or 
defendants for trial, the Tribal Judge may order separate trials, grant a severance of defendants, or 
provide any other relief as justice may require.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Notice of alibi. 
 
(a) At the time of, or subsequent to arraignment, the defendant may request the prosecutor to 
provide a written statement of the time, date, and place at which the alleged offense was committed. 
The prosecutor shall provide the defendant with the requested information within five (5) days of 
receiving the defendant's request. 
 
(b) Within ten (10) days of receiving the written statement from the prosecutor, or at such 
time as the Tribal Judge may direct, the defendant shall serve a written notice upon the prosecutor 
stating the defendant's intention to offer the defense of alibi.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Motion for continuance. The defendant or the Colony may file a written motion
text:
for continuance, or the court may continue the proceedings on its own motion. If a party so moves 
less than 10 days before a scheduled hearing or trial, the Tribal Court may require the motion to be 
supported by an affidavit, whether or not the motion is opposed by the adverse party. This section, 
however, shall be applied in a manner which insures criminal cases are tried with due diligence 
consistent with the rights of the defendant to a speedy trial.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Pretrial conference. 
 
(a) Any party may move the Tribal Court for one or more conferences to consider such 
matters as will promote a fair and expedient trial. 
 
(b) In the interest of justice, the Tribal Court may order a pretrial conference based on its 
own motion. 
 

30 
 
 
(c) At the conclusion of any pretrial conference, the presiding judge shall prepare and file a 
memorandum of the matters agreed upon. No admissions made by the defendant or defendant's 
counsel at the conference shall be used against the defendant unless the admissions are reduced to 
writing and signed by the defendant and the defendant's counsel. 
 
(d) In the interest of judicial economy, the Court may order the parties to prepare a proposed 
Pretrial Order, without a pretrial conference, for the Court's signature.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Pretrial diversion. 
 
(a) At any time the prosecutor and a defendant who has counsel or how has voluntarily 
waived counsel may agree to the deferral of a prosecution for a specified period of time based on one 
or more of the following conditions: 
(1) that the defendant may not commit any offense; 
(2) that the defendant may not engage in specified activities, conduct, and 
associations bearing a relationship to the conduct upon which the charge against the defendant is 
based; 
(3) that the defendant shall participate in a supervised rehabilitation program, which 
may include treatment, counseling, training, or education; 
(4) that the defendant shall make restitution in a specified manner for harm or loss 
caused by the offense; or 
(5) any other reasonable conditions, including voluntary exclusion from the Colony. 
 
(b) The agreement must be in writing, must be signed by the parties, and must state that the 
defendant waives the right to speedy trial for the period of deferral. The agreement may include 
stipulations concerning the admissibility of evidence, specified testimony, or depositions if the 
deferral of the prosecution is terminated and there is a trial on the charge. 
 
(c) The prosecution must be deferred for a period specified in the agreement unless there has 
been a violation of its terms. 
 
(d) The agreement must be terminated and the prosecution automatically dismissed with 
prejudice upon expiration and compliance with the terms of the agreement.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: When depositions may be taken,
text:
(a) A deposition may be taken if it appears that a positive witness: 
(1) is likely to be either unable to attend or otherwise prevented from attending a trial 
or hearing; 
(2) absent from the state at the time of the trial or hearing; or 
(3) is unwilling to provide relevant information to a requesting party and the witness's 
testimony is material and necessary in order to prevent a failure of justice. The Court shall, upon 
motion of any party and proper notice, order that the testimony of the witness be taken by deposition 
and that any designated books, papers, documents, or tangible objects, not privileged, be introduced 
at the time the deposition is taken. 

31 
 
 
(b) The witness whose deposition is to be taken may be required by subpoena to attend at any 
place designated by the Tribal Court, taking into account the convenience of the parties and of the 
witness. 
 
(c) If it appears upon the affidavit of counsel for a party that good cause exists to believe that 
a witness will not respond to a subpoena and the administration of justice requires, a judge may issue 
an arrest warrant commanding the arrest of a material witness. The arrest warrant must further order 
a deposition to be taken without unnecessary delay. A person may not be imprisoned for the purpose 
of securing testimony in any criminal proceeding longer than necessary to take the person's 
deposition.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Procedure for taking deposition. 
 
(a) The party at whose instance a deposition is taken shall give to every other party 
reasonable written notice of the time and place for taking such deposition. The notice must state the 
name and address of each person to be examined. On motion of the party upon whom the notice is 
served, the court for cause shown may extend or shorten the time or change the place for taking the 
deposition. 
 
(b) A deposition must be taken in the manner provided in civil actions, and the scope and 
manner of examination and cross-examination must be restricted as would be allowed in the trial 
itself. 
 
(c) The deposition must be filed with the Tribal Court making the order and held until the 
trial. Either party shall make available to the other party or the other party's counsel for examination 
and use at the taking of the deposition any relevant, non-privileged statement of the witness being 
deposed that is the possession of either party. 
 
(d) Objections to deposition testimony or evidence may be reserved for subsequent 
determination by the Tribal Court. 
 
(e) Unless a defendant in custody has waived, in writing, the right to be present at the taking
