of a deposition, the officer having custody of the defendant must be notified of the time and place set 
for the deposition. The officer having custody shall produce the defendant and keep the defendant in 
the presents of a witness during the deposition. 
 
(f) A defendant not in custody who fails to appear, without good cause, at the taking of the 
deposition after being notified of the time and place set for the deposition will be considered to have 
waived the right to be present. The waiver includes a waiver of any objection to the taking and use of 
the deposition based upon that right. 
 
(g) Whenever a deposition is taken at the instance of the prosecution or whenever a 
deposition is taken at the instance of a defendant who is unable to bear the expense of taking a 
deposition, the Court shall direct that the cost of the transcript of the deposition, the Court shall 
direct that the cost of the transcript of the deposition be paid by the Colony. 
 

32
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Use of depositions at trial. Any deposition may be used by any party for the 
purpose allowed by the Rules of Evidence set forth in this Law and Order Code.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Subpoenas. The Tribal Court has the power to issue subpoenas to compel the
text:
attendance of witnesses and the production of documents either on the Tribal Court’s own motion or 
on the request of any party to a case, which shall bear the signature of the Clerk of Court or Assistant 
Clerk issuing the subpoena. The subpoenas may direct the attendance of witnesses or the 
production of documents or evidence at a specified date, time and location. Subpoenas under this 
section may be issued for purposes of discovery, for pretrial hearing, or for a trial or post trial 
proceeding. 
 
Part 10. Mental Disorder
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Mental disorder precluding fitness to proceed. A person who, as a result of a
text:
mental disorder, is unable to understand the proceedings against the person or to assist in the 
person's own defense may not be tried, convicted, or sentenced for the commission of an offense so 
long as the incapacity endures.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Evidence of mental disorder admissible as an affirmative defense. Evidence
text:
that the defendant suffered from a mental disorder is admissible to prove that the defendant could not 
appreciate the criminality of his conduct. This is an affirmative defense which the defendant has the 
burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Examination of defendant. 
 
(a) If the defendant or the defendant's counsel makes a motion requesting an examination or 
if the issue of the defendant's fitness to proceed is raised by the Tribal Court, prosecution, or defense 
counsel, the court shall appoint at least one qualified psychiatrist or licensed clinical psychologist to 
examine and report upon the defendant's mental condition. 
 
(b) In the examination, any method may be employed that is accepted by the medical or 
psychological profession for the examination of those alleged to be suffering from a mental disorder. 
The cost of the examination must be paid by the Colony. 
 
(c) The examiner shall be permitted to have reasonable access to the defendant for purpose 
of the examination.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Report of examination. 
 
(a) A report of the examination must include: 
(1) a description of the nature of the examination; 
(2) a diagnosis of the mental condition of the defendant, including an opinion as to 
the defendant suffers from a mental disorder and may require commitment or has a disability that is 
expected to continue indefinitely that is attributable to mental retardation, or related neurological 
conditions or illnesses; 

33 
 
 
(3) if the defendant suffers from a mental disorder, an opinion as to the defendant's 
capacity to understand the proceedings against the defendant to assist in the defendant's own 
defense; 
(4) an opinion as to the capacity of the defendant to have a particular state of mind 
that is an element of the offense charged; and 
(5) an opinion as to the capacity of the defendant, because of mental disorder, to 
appreciate the criminality of the defendant's conduct. 
 
(b) If the examination cannot be conducted by reason of the unwillingness of the defendant to 
participate in the examination, the report must state that fact and must include, if possible, an 
opinion as to whether unwillingness of the defendant was the result of a mental disorder.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Determination of fitness to proceed. 
 
(a) When the issue is raised by the Tribal Court, the defendant or defendant's counsel, or by 
the prosecutor, the Court must determine whether the defendant is fit to proceed. If neither the 
prosecution nor the defense contest the finding of the report, the court may make the determination 
on the basis of the report. If the finding is contested, the Tribal Court shall hold a hearing on the 
issue. If the report is received in evidence, the parties have the right to subpoena and cross-examine 
the psychiatrist or licensed clinical psychologist who joined in the report and to offer evidence upon 
the issue. 
 
(b) If the court determines that the defendant lacks fitness to proceed, the proceeding against 
the defendant must be suspended and the court may commit the defendant to an appropriate 
institution for so long as the unfitness endures. 
 
(c) The court shall review the defendant's fitness to proceed within 90 days of the 
determination that the defendant was unfit to proceed. If the court finds that the defendant is still 
unfit to proceed and that it does not appear that the defendant will become fit to proceed in the 
reasonably foreseeable future, the proceeding against the defendant must be dismissed without 
prejudice. 
 
(d) The expenses of sending the defendant to an appropriate institution, of keeping the 
defendant there, and of bringing the defendant back are chargeable to the Colony.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Proceedings if fitness regained. When the Tribal Court, upon its own motion or
text:
application of the prosecution or defense for a hearing on the issue, determines that the defendant 
has regained fitness to proceed, the proceeding must be resumed. If, however, the court is of the 
view that so much time has elapsed since the commitment of the defendant that it would be unjust to 
resume the criminal proceedings, the court may dismiss the charge and may order the defendant to 
be discharged, or subject to the law governing the civil commitment of persons suffering from 
mental illness, order the defendant committed to an appropriate institution.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Psychiatric or psychological testimony at trial. 
(a) At trial, any psychiatrist or clinical psychologist who reported under this part may be 
called as a witness by the prosecution or defense. 

34 
 
 
 
(b) Both the prosecution and the defense may summon any other qualified psychiatrist or 
clinical psychologist to testify, but no one who has not examined the defendant is competent to 
testify to an expert opinion with respect to the mental condition of the defendant. An expert who 
has not examined the defendant may, however, testify to the validity of the procedure followed by or 
the general scientific propositions stated by another witness. 
 
(c) Any testifying expert may be cross-examined as to any matter bearing on the expert's 
competency or credibility or the validity of the expert's examination or medical or psychological 
diagnosis or opinion.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Admissibility of statements made during examination or treatment. A
text:
statement made for the purpose of psychiatric or psychological examination or treatment by a person 
subjected to examination or treatment is not admissible in evidence against the person at trial on any 
issue other than that of the person's mental condition. It is admissible on the issue of the person's 
mental condition only when and after the defendant presents evidence that due to a mental disorder 
the defendant could not appreciate the criminality of his or her conduct.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Commitment or release upon finding of not guilty by reason of mental
text:
disorder. 
 
(a) When a defendant is found not guilty for the reason that due to a mental disorder the 
defendant could not appreciate the criminality of his conduct, the court shall order a predisposition 
investigation to determine the present mental condition of the defendant. The court may hold a 
hearing to obtain additional testimony or evidence to make its determination. 
 
(b) If the offense with which the defendant was charged involved a substantial risk of serious 
bodily injury or death, or actual bodily injury, the Tribal Court may find that the defendant suffers 
from a mental disorder that renders the defendant a danger to the defendant or others and order the 
prosecution to initiate civil commitment proceedings. 
 
(c) If the charge did not involve a substantial risk of serious bodily injury or death, or actual 
bodily injury, the court shall release the defendant. 
 
Part 11. Trial
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Right to a jury trial. 
 
(a) Defendants in all criminal cases classified A, B or C shall have a right to trial by jury of 
six fair and impartial jurors. 
 
(b) A defendant may waive the right to a jury trial. Such waiver must be in writing.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Priority of the tribal court calendar. 
(a) Prosecutions against defendants held in custody must be disposed of in advance of 
prosecutions against defendants released on bail, unless otherwise directed by the Tribal Court. 

35 
 
 
(b) Criminal actions take precedence over civil actions when determining a hearing date.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Questions of law and fact. 
 
(a) Issues of fact shall be submitted to the jurors, unless the defendant has waived her or his 
right to a jury trial, in which case issues of fact shall be submitted to the judge. 
 
(b) All questions of law must be decided by the trial judge.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Trial preparation time. The defendant is entitled to reasonable time, as
text: determined by the judge, to prepare for trial after entering a plea of not guilty.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Order of trial. 
 
(a) In a jury trial, after selecting and impaneling the jurors, the Tribal Court shall state the 
nature of the charges and generally instruct the jurors as to their duties. 
 
(b) Unless waived, both the prosecution and the defendant will be afforded an opportunity to 
make an opening statement prior to the presentation of any evidence or testimony. The defendant 
may reserve her or his opening statement until after the prosecution has presented its case-in-chief. 
 
(c) After presenting an opening statement, the prosecution must present evidence and offer 
testimony supporting the allegations contained in the charging document. The defendant shall be 
given an opportunity to cross-examine any witness called by the prosecution. 
 
(d) Once the prosecution has rested its case, the defendant may give any reserved opening 
statement and present any defenses or evidence relating to the allegations contained in the charging 
document. The prosecution shall be given an opportunity to cross-examine any witness called by the 
defendant. 
 
(e) Rebuttal evidence may be presented after the conclusion of the defense case when 
appropriate as determined by the trial judge, and, if necessary, surrebuttal evidence may be offered 
by the defense. 
 
(f) No new evidence may be presented after both the prosecution and defendant have rested 
their case, unless allowed by the trial judge in the interests of justice. 
 
(g) After the close of evidence and either before or after the closing statements are 
presented, the specific instructions, as submitted in writing by the prosecutor and defendant, shall 
either be: 

36 
 
 
(1) given as requested or proposed by counsel; 
(2) refused based on stated grounds; or 
(3) given with modification. 
 
All instructions shall be filed as part of the record. 
 
(h) Either prior or subsequent to the reading of the jury instructions, the prosecution and the 
defense may make a closing statement. The prosecution precedes the defense and may also make a 
rebuttal closing statement. 
 
(i) The trier of fact shall render a decision after the conclusion of the case. If the case is tried 
to a judge, the verdict shall set forth the court's findings of fact, conclusions of law and a judgment 
of guilty or not guilty. If the case is tried to a jury, the verdict shall be guilty or not guilty in 
accordance with the facts and the jury instructions.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Insufficient evidence. If the Tribal Court determines at the close of the
text:
prosecution's case in chief, or at the conclusion of the case, that the evidence presented is insufficient 
to sustain a conviction of the charged offense or offenses, the Tribal Court may, on its own motion 
or on the motion of the defense, dismiss the action and discharge the defendant. No new trial may be 
granted unless the judgment of acquittal is vacated or reversed on appeal. 
 
Part 12. Juries
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Qualification of jurors. Any person who is an enrolled Tribal member of the
text: Colony and is qualified to vote in elections of the Tribal Council is an eligible juror.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Formation of jury. {Amended by Resolution No. 2006-RS-60 on 7/18/06.}
text:
(a) Definition of Jury: A jury is a body of six persons selected under the RSIC Law and 
Order Code, from the pool of eligible jurors to decide questions of fact and return a verdict, in 
accordance with jury instructions as to applicable law, in the case submitted to them. Eligible jurors 
must be enrolled members of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony who are qualified to vote in elections 
of the Tribal Council. 
 
(b) Selection of Jury Pool: 
 
(1) The Clerk of the Court shall obtain the most recent list of person qualified to vote 
in the elections of the Tribal Council, and shall submit such list to the Tribal Court Administrator; 
 
(2) The Tribal Court Administrator shall summon a jury pool, at random, of at least 
20 people from the list of qualified voters; 
 
(3) If a person is chosen at random who has been summoned to jury duty at any time 
during the past 12 months, that person shall be automatically excused, and another person shall be 
randomly selected; 
 
(4) Any person who is a current member of the Tribal Court staff or the Tribal Police 
Department shall be exempt from jury service; 
 
(5) A person may be excused from jury duty upon written request if that person: 
 
 
(A) is over 70 years of age; 

37 
 
 
 
 
(B) is physically or mentally disabled; or 
 
 
(C) lives more than 65 miles away from the Tribal Court; or 
 
 
(D) has an emergency or other extenuating circumstance approved by the 
Tribal Court Administrator. 
 
(6) Any person summoned to jury duty shall have a minimum of fifteen days from the 
date of service of the summons in which to report or to file a written request with the Tribal Court 
Administrator to be excused. 
 
(7) Any person summoned to jury duty who fails to appear pursuant to the summons 
and fails to show good cause will be in contempt of court and shall be fined no more than $100.00. 
 
(c) Seating of Jury. Six jurors shall be selected in accordance with the requirements of this 
Part to be seated as the jury. The six persons selected shall be sworn in as jurors. One alternate 
juror shall be seated, but shall not serve on the jury unless one of the selected jurors is excused or 
discharged. If no juror is excused or discharged, the alternate juror shall be excused when the jury 
retires to consider its verdict.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Motion to discharge a jury panel. 
 
(a) Any objection to the manner in which a jury panel has been selected or drawn shall be 
raised by a motion to discharge the jury panel. The motion shall be made at least (5) five days prior 
to the trial date. 
 
(b) The motion shall be made in writing supported by an affidavit and shall state facts which 
slow that the jury panel was improperly selected or drawn. 
 
(c) If the motion states facts which show that the jury panel has been improperly selected or 
drawn, it shall be the duty of the Tribal Court to conduct a hearing. The burden of proof shall be on 
the movant. 
 
(d) If the Tribal Court finds that the jury panel was improperly selected or drawn, the court 
shall order the jury panel discharged and the selection or drawing of a new panel consistent with the 
provisions of this code.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Examination of prospective jurors. 
 
(a) After sending summons, but at least five (5) days before trial, the Clerk of Court shall 
make available to the involved parties a list of prospective jurors. 
 
(b) At the time of trial, the initial questioning of the jurors for the purpose of voir dire shall 
be conducted by the judge in order to determine whether each prospective juror is capable of being a 
fair and impartial juror. Specific questions to be asked the jurors may include, but are not limited to, 
whether any juror: 
(1) is directly related to any party involved in the action, including but not limited to 
the defendant, advocate, attorney, or any prospective witness; 
(2) is involved in any business, financial, professional, or personal relationship with 
any of the involved parties or alleged victim or defendant; 

38 
 
 
(3) has had any previous legal dealings with any of the involved parties or alleged 
victim; 
(4) has served as a juror or been a witness on a previous trial involving the same 
parties; 
(5) has any vested interest in the outcome of the action before the court; 
(6) has formed an opinion of the defendant's guilt; and 
(7) has the belief that the punishment fixed by law is too severe for the offense 
charged. 
 
(c) Any prospective juror whom the Tribal Court determines incapable of acting with 
impartiality and without prejudice to the substantial rights of either party shall be excused. 
 
(d) After questioning by the judge, the prosecutor and defendant or defense counsel may 
question the prospective jurors to determine impartiality. The judge may limit the prosecutor's and 
defendant's or defense counsel's examination of any prospective jurors when the judge believes such 
examination to be improper.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Challenges. 
 
(a) The prosecution and defense shall have unlimited challenges for cause. Each challenge 
must be tried and determined by the Tribal Court at the time the challenge is made. 
 
(b) The prosecution and defense shall have three (3) peremptory challenges and one (1) 
peremptory challenge in the event that an alternate juror is selected, unless a lesser number is agreed 
to by the parties in writing. 
 
(c) All challenges must be made to the Tribal Court before the jury is sworn. When a 
potential challenge for cause is discovered after the jury is sworn and before the introduction of any 
evidence, the Tribal Court may allow a challenge for cause to be made.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Conduct of jury during trial. 
 
(a) Once impaneled, jurors shall be instructed by the judge that it is their duty not to 
converse among themselves or with anyone else on any subject connected with the trial, or to form 
or express any opinion thereon, until the issues of the case are finally submitted to them. 
 
(b) At each adjournment, prior to submission of the case to the jury, the judge shall instruct 
the jurors as to whether they may separate or must remain in the care of the bailiff or other proper 
officer of the court. 
 
(c) Jurors shall be further instructed that they are prohibited form conversing with any of the 
parties connected with the trial until after a verdict has been reached.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
View of relevant place or property. 
(a) Upon request by the prosecution or defense, the Tribal Court may allow the jury to view 
any place or property deemed pertinent to the just determination of the case. 

39 
 
 
(b) If viewing of a place or property is deemed appropriate, the Tribal Court shall place the 
jury under the custody of the bailiff, or other proper officer of the court, who shall then transport the 
jury to the viewing place. 
 
(c) The place or property will be shown to the jury by a person appointed by the Tribal Court 
for that purpose, and the jurors may personally inspect the same. 
 
(d) The bailiff, or other proper officer of the court, must insure that no person speaks or 
otherwise communicates with the jury, on any subject connected with the trial, while viewing the 
place or property or traveling to or from the viewing site. 
 
(e) After the jury has viewed the place or property, the bailiff, or other proper officer of the 
Tribal Court, shall return the jurors to the courtroom without unnecessary delay or at a specified 
time, as directed by the court.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Jury Instructions. 
 
(a) General instructions may be furnished by the Tribal Court. When either the defendant or 
the prosecutor desires a special instruction to be given to the jury, such proposed instruction shall be 
reduced to writing, signed by the party offering the instruction and delivered to the judge at least 5 
days before trial unless a different time is ordered by the judge. For good cause shown, the parties 
may supplement or withdraw instructions at the close of evidence. 
 
(b) All jury instructions shall adequately inform the jurors of: 
(1) which decisions are made by the jury and which by the presiding judge; 
(2) the issues of fact in the case; 
(3) the rules of law to be applied to the issues of fact; 
(4) the burden of proof with respect to each issue of fact; and 
(5) the proof needed to discharge that burden. 
 
(c) The party not offering a proposed instruction shall be allowed reasonable opportunity to 
examine the proposed instruction and object to it. The objection must specifically state on what 
grounds the instruction is not an accurate statement of the law or is not an appropriate instruction for 
this particular case and, therefore, should not be given. 
 
(d) A dispute regarding a proposed jury instruction must be settled outside of the jury's 
presence by the court which may hold a settlement hearing. 
 
 
(e) A record must be made at a hearing to settle instructions. 
 
(f) A party may not appeal as error any portion of the instructions or omission from the 
instructions unless an objection was made specifically stating the matter objected to, and the grounds 
for the objection, at the settlement of instructions of in writing prior to a settlement hearing. 
 
(g) The presence of the defendant is not required during the settlement of instructions. 
 

40 
 
 
(h) After all evidence has been presented, and before closing arguments, the court shall give 
both general and specific instructions to the jurors. 
 
(i) For the record, but not for the jury, the court shall mark or endorse each instruction in 
such a mariner that it shall distinctly appear what proposed instruction were rejected, what were 
given in whole and what were modified, together with the court's reasons for given as requested, as 
modified, or refusing a proposed instruction. 
 
(j) All proposed instructions are part of the court record. All objections to jury instructions 
must be noted on the court record, as well as the Tribal Court's reasons for either giving as 
requested, as modified, or refusing a proposed instruction.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Jury Deliberations. 
 
(a) After closing arguments, the Tribal Court shall commit the jury to the care of the bailiff 
or other officer of the court who shall keep the jurors together and prevent communication between 
the jurors and others. 
 
(b) Upon retiring to deliberate, the jurors shall select a juror as foreperson. 
 
(c) After the jury has retired for deliberation, if there is any disagreement among the jurors 
as to the testimony or if the jurors desire to be informed on any point of law arising in the course, 
they shall notify the bailiff or the officer appointed to keep them together, who shall then notify the 
court. The information requested may be given, in the discretion of the court, after consultation with 
the parties.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Items allowed in the jury room. Upon retiring for deliberation, the jurors may
text:
take with them the written jury instructions read by the court, notes of the proceedings taken by 
themselves, and all exhibits that have been received as evidence in the cause that in the opinion of 
the court will be necessary.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Form of verdict. 
 
(a) The jury shall return a verdict as instructed by the court and for each offense charged. 
The verdict must be unanimous in all criminal actions. The verdict must be signed by the foreperson 
and returned by the jury to the judge in open court. 
 
(b) When two or more defendants are involved in the case before the jury , the jurors may 
reach a verdict regarding any one of the defendants. If the jury cannot agree with respect to all the 
defendants, the defendant or defendants as to whom it does not agree may be tried again.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Polling the jury. When a verdict is returned, but before it is recorded, the jury 
shall be polled at the request of any party or upon the court's own motion. If the results of the poll 
show that the verdict does not reflect unanimous concurrence by each juror, the jury may be directed 
to return for further deliberations or may be discharged at the court's discretion. 
 

41
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Conviction of lesser-included offense. 
 
(a) When it appears to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant has committed 
an offense but there is reasonable doubt as to whether he or she is guilty of the given offense or one 
or more lesser included offenses as provided in subsection (b) of this section, he or she may only be 
convicted of the greatest included offense about which there is no reasonable doubt. 
 
(b) The defendant may be found guilty of a lesser-included offense which is either an 
offense which is necessarily included in the offense charged or is an attempt to commit either the 
offense charged or an offense necessarily included therein. 
 
(c) A lesser-included offense instruction must be given when there is a proper request by one 
of the parties and the jury, based on the evidence, could be warranted in finding the defendant guilty 
of a lesser included offense. 
 
(d) When a lesser-included offense instruction is given, the court shall instruct the jury that it 
must reach a verdict on the crime charged before it may proceed to a lesser included offense. Upon 
request of the defendant at the settling of instructions, the court shall instruct the jury that it may 
consider the lesser included offense if it is unable after reasonable effort to reach a verdict on the 
greater offense.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Discharging jurors. When the jury has reached a verdict or has determined that it
text:
is unable to either acquit or find the defendant guilty, even with additional deliberation, the court 
shall discharge the jurors from service.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Jury Fees. Each juror who is called to serve or serves on a jury shall be paid a 
reasonable fee for each day of service, and for transportation costs to and from the Tribal Court. 
Such sums shall be set by the Tribal Council. 
 
Part 13. Post-Trial and Sentencing Procedures
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Motion for new trial. 
 
(a) Within twenty (20) days of a guilty verdict the defendant may file a written motion with 
the court requesting a new trial. The motion must specify the grounds upon which the request is 
made. 
 
(b) After hearing the motion for a new trial, the Tribal Judge may in the interest of 
justice: 
(1) deny the motion; 
(2) grant a new trial; or 
(3) modify or change the verdict or findings by finding the defendant guilty of a 
lesser included offense or not guilty. 
 
(c) If the motion for a new trial is granted, the issues presented in the first trial shall be tried 
before the same judge, but by a different jury, as if there had never been a previous trial. 

42
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Rendering judgment and pronouncing sentence. 
 
(a) The judgment shall be rendered in open court. 
 
(b) If acquitted after trial, judgment shall be rendered immediately and the defendant shall be 
discharged from custody or from any conditions of release, and any bail posted shall be exonerated. 
 
(c) Upon a verdict or finding guilt, the Tribal Court may do any of the following: 
(1) immediately determine sentence; 
(2) designate a future sentencing date to hear the issue of sentencing; or 
(3) order that within thirty (30) days from the date trial was completed or a guilty or 
no contest plea was given, a pre-sentence investigation report be prepared and filed with the Court 
and copies provided not less than five (5) days prior to the date set for sentencing. 
 
(d) The determination and imposition of sentence and judgment are the exclusive duty of the 
Tribal Judge acting within his/her discretion. 
 
(e) No sentence shall be imposed until: 
(1) the defendant has had an opportunity to examine any pre-sentence investigative 
report and cross-examine the preparer of such report on the basis for any sentencing 
recommendations contained in the report; 
(2) the prosecution and defense have had an opportunity to present evidence, 
witnesses, and an argument regarding the appropriateness of a sentencing option; and 
(3) the defendant has had the opportunity to speak on his or her own behalf and to 
present any information likely to mitigate the pending sentence. 
 
(f) Upon pronouncing the sentence, the judge shall: 
(1) clearly state the reasons for the sentence; 
(2) sign the sentencing order; and 
(3) enter the sentence into the Tribal Court's record. 
 
(g) After imposing sentence, the Tribal Judge shall inform the defendant of his right to 
appeal.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure
Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure
Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Execution of sentence. 
 
(a) If a sentence of imprisonment in imposed, the Tribal Judge shall transmit a certified copy 
of the disposition to Tribal law enforcement stating the length of sentence and any conditions or 
exceptions relating to the sentence. The defendant shall be discharged after satisfactorily fulfilling 
the requirements of the imposed sentence. 
 
(b) If judgment is rendered imposing a fine only, the defendant must be discharged after 
making acceptable arrangements to pay the fine within the period of time specified by the Tribal 
Court, not exceeding two (2) years. The Tribal Judge may also allow the defendant to perform 
community service for the Colony's benefit to offset any fine or allow the defendant to be 
imprisoned until the fine is satisfied, applying $40.00 for every day served. If no such permission is 
included in the sentence, the fine or court costs shall be paid prior to formal release. 
 
(c) If judgment is rendered imposing both imprisonment and a fine, the defendant shall be 
discharged after fulfilling the requirements of subsections (a) and (b) of this section.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Restitution. 
 
(a) When restitution is ordered, the Tribal Judge shall specify the amount, method and 
payment schedule imposed upon the offender. 
 
(b) Before restitution may be ordered, the defendant shall receive notice of the amount and 
terms requested and shall be entitled to a hearing upon his or her timely request. 

44 
 
 
(c) The fact that restitution was ordered is not admissible as evidence in a civil action and 
has no legal effect on the merits of a civil action. 
 
(d) Any restitution paid by the defendant to an injured person must be deducted from any 
monetary award granted to the injured person in a civil action arising out of the facts or events which 
were the basis for the restitution. The court trying the civil action shall determine the amount of any 
possible reduction due to payment of restitution by the defendant under this section. However, in the 
event that criminal and civil actions against an offender arising from the same transaction or events 
are heard in courts of different jurisdictions, one of which is the Tribal Court, the Tribal Court shall 
adjust the defendant's payments within its jurisdictional control for restitution or otherwise to assure 
that an injured person does not recover twice for the same harm. 
 
(e) A defendant may petition for modification of any sentence imposing restitution and 
request a hearing on the matter. The injured person shall be given notice of any proposed 
modifications and afforded an opportunity to be heard on the proposed modification.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Payment of fines and restitution. 
 
(a) All monies collected as the result of a fine imposed by the Tribal Court shall be paid 
through the Tribal Clerk of Court. Upon receiving the monies, the clerk shall: 
(1) issue a receipt to the paying party; 
(2) credit the account of the offender, noting whether the fine is paid in full or what 
balance, if any, remains due; and 
(3) transfer the monies to the general fund of the Colony, unless otherwise 
specifically directed by a provision of this Code. 
 
(b) All monies collected due to an order of restitution shall be paid through the Tribal Clerk 
of Court. Upon receiving the monies, the clerk shall: 
(1) issue a receipt to the paying party; and 
(2) credit the account of the offender, noting whether the restitution is paid in full or 
what balance, if any, remains due; and 
(3) transfer the monies to the party ordered to receive restitution payments.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Failure to pay fine or restitution. 
 
(a) If a defendant fails to pay a fine or restitution as ordered, the Tribal Court or prosecutor 
may move that the defendant show cause as to why the defendant's nonpayment should not be 
treated as contempt of court. 
 
(b) Notice of a show cause hearing on the contempt charge shall be served on the offender 
by law enforcement officers at least five days prior to the date set for hearing. Notice shall also be 
served on the victim if the show cause was issued for failure to pay restitution. 
 
(c) Unless the offender shows that the nonpayment was not attributable to an intentional 
refusal to obey a Tribal Court order of the offender's failure to make a good faith effort to make the 
ordered payments, the Tribal Court may find the offender in contempt and order the person 

45 
 
 
incarcerated until the fine or restitution is satisfied. Time served shall be credited against the fine at 
the rate of $40.00 per day. 
 
(d) If the Tribal Court determines that the offender's nonpayment does not constitute 
contempt, the Tribal Court may modify the original sentence, judgment, or order, allowing the 
offender additional time to pay the fine or restitution or reducing the amount owed.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Revocation of suspended or deferred sentence. 
 
(a) If a petition requesting revocation has been filed and a revocation hearing held, the Tribal 
Court may revoke a defendant's suspended or deferred sentence if a preponderance of the evidence 
shows that the imposed conditions of the sentence have been violated. 
 
(b) A petition seeking revocation of a suspended or deferred sentence must be filed during 
the period of suspension or deferral, or within five (5) days after the period of suspension or deferral 
ends if the offender's violation of a condition of probation occurred with the final 48 hours prior to 
the end of the period. Expiration of the time ordered under a suspended or deferred sentence, prior to 
a hearing for revocation, does not deprive the Tribal Court of jurisdiction to rule on the revocation 
petition.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Dismissal and expungement after deferred sentence. Whenever the Tribal
text:
Judge has deferred the imposition of sentence and after expiration of the deferral period and after the 
defendant's successful completion of any conditions of deferral, upon motion by the court, the 
defendant, or defendant's counsel, the Tribal Judge shall allow the defendant to withdraw his or her 
plea of guilty or strike the verdict of guilty from the record and order that the charge or charges 
against the defendant be dismissed and expunged from his or her record.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Credit for time served. If a defendant has served any of the defendant's sentence
text:
under a commitment based upon a judgment that is subsequently declared invalid or that is modified 
during the term of imprisonment, the time served must be credited against any subsequent sentence 
received upon a new commitment for the same criminal act or acts.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Credit for incarceration prior to conviction. 
 
(a) Except as provided in paragraph (c), any person incarcerated on a bailable offense and 
against whom a judgment of imprisonment is rendered must be allowed credit for each day of 
incarceration prior to sentencing, except that the time allowed as a credit may not exceed the term of 
the prison sentence rendered. 
 
(b) Any person incarcerated on a bailable offense who does not supply bail and against 
whom a fine is levied on conviction of the offense must be allowed a credit for each day of 
incarceration prior to conviction, except that the amount allowed or credited may not exceed the 
amount of the fine. The daily rate of credit for incarceration is $40.00 per day. 
 
(c) No days credit for incarceration shall be allowed for any days a defendant is being held 
by a foreign jurisdiction and is not available to appear in person in Tribal Court. 

46 
 
 
Part 14. Parole
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Eligibility for parole. 
 
(a) Any person confined to a correctional facility used by the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony, 
who has continuously served at least one-half of the imposed sentence is eligible for parole. 
 
(b) Parole shall only be granted when the sentencing judge determines the person's release 
will not be detrimental to the offender or the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony community and it is in the 
best interest of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony community. Parole shall not be given as an award of 
clemency or a reduction of sentence.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Eligibility hearing. 
 
(a) Any person confined to a correctional facility used by the Colony, who has continuously 
served at least one-half of the imposed sentence, may file written request with the Tribal Court for a 
hearing regarding possible parole. 
 
(b) All persons desiring to speak at such hearing shall be heard, including, but not limited to: 
(1) Law enforcement; 
(2) The Colony prosecutor; 
(3) Family and friends of the designated offender; 
(4) The designated offender; and 
(5) The Colony tribal advocate or defense counsel. 
 
(c) The Tribal Court shall consider all pertinent information regarding the designated 
offender, including but not limited to the following: 
(1) The circumstances and nature of the offense; 
(2) Past criminal record; 
(3) Past employment record; 
(4) Conduct during imprisonment; and 
(5) The results of any physical or psychological reports. 
(6) Attending classes or completing programs in substance abuse (including self-help 
programs), domestic violence, parenting, education towards obtaining a degree or General Education 
Diploma (GED) or any other certified class or program which would assist the offender to be a 
productive individual after release.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Conditions of release. 
 
(a) Every offender released on parole shall remain in the legal custody of the Colony's 
correctional officer, subject to the conditions imposed by the Tribal Court. 
 
(b) The order granting parole shall specifically set forth: 
(1) the duration of parole; 
(2) the conditions of parole; 
(3) the party designated to monitor or supervise the person paroled; and 

47 
 
 
(4) consequences of parole and parole violation.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

text:
Violation of parole. 
 
(a) Any person released on parole may be arrested upon warrant or served notice to appear 
for violating a condition of parole. 
 
(b) The person released on parole must show cause why the alleged violation should not be 
considered sufficient to revoke parole.
heading_path: Title III CRIMINAL CODE > Chapter 1 — Criminal Procedure

heading: Purpose and construction. The provisions of this chapter shall be construed in
text:
accordance with the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony Tribal customs as well as to achieve the 
following general principles and purposes: 
(a) 
To forbid and prevent the commission of offenses and give fair warning of 
conduct which is declared by the laws of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony to be an 
offense; 
(b) 
To adequately define the conduct and mental states which constitute an offense 
and to safeguard permitted conduct; 
(c) 
To prescribe penalties which are proportionate to the seriousness of the offense 
and which permit recognition of differing rehabilitative needs of individuals 
offenders while at the same time recognizing the need of the entire Reno-Sparks 
Indian Colony and individual members for protection from offenders; 
(d) 
To prevent arbitrary and oppressive treatment of persons accused or convicted of 
offenses and to promote the correction and rehabilitation of such persons; and 
(e) 
To protect any person whose health and welfare may be adversely affected or 
threatened due to abuse, neglect or exploitation by family, household members, or 
other person in a legal or contractual position of providing physical, mental or 
medical assistance and support to the affected person. 
(f) 
For purposes of clarity, wherever in this Code the masculine pronoun “he” is 
used, it is to be understood to refer to persons of either gender.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

heading: Civil actions not barred. The Code of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony does
text:
not bar, suspend or otherwise affect any right or liability to damages, penalty, forfeiture, or other 
remedy authorized by law to be recovered. Civil injury is not merged into a criminal offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

heading: Enforcement procedures for civil infractions. Non-Indians violating a Class
text:
A, B or C offense in this Title or any RSIC Ordinance on Colony lands shall be subject to the 
following enforcement procedures: 
(a) 
Citations. 
(1) 
Initial Proceedings. Proceedings may be initiated by issuing a citation to 
the defendant. A copy of the citation shall be filed with the Clerk of Court 
and a second copy shall be retained by the citing officer. When filed with 
the Clerk of Court, the citation shall serve as a civil complaint. 
(2) 
Issuance. The citation shall be personally issued to the defendant. 
(3) 
Contents. The citation shall contain at least the following: 
(i) 
The name, address, phone number and date of birth of the 
defendant, if available; 
(ii) 
The date and time of the alleged offense; 
(iii) 
The particular section of this Title alleged to have been violated; 
(iv) 
The notice requiring the defendant to appear in Tribal Court on a 
stated date and at a stated time; 
(v) 
The defendant may sign the citation and thereby promise to appear 
in Tribal Court, 
(vi) 
A statement of the maximum fine for each violation alleged. 
 
(b) 
Alternative Citation. A defendant may be transferred to other governments for 
prosecution under applicable laws if he refuses to sign the citation consenting to 
Tribal jurisdiction and promising to appear in Tribal Court, or, after signing the 
citation, the defendant fails to appear at the Tribal Court hearing. 
 
(c) 
The Tribal Court shall conduct without necessary delay an admit/deny hearing for 
all citations issued under this Section and advise the charged person that he or she 
has a right to a civil adjudicatory hearing. 
 
(d) 
If the cited party knowingly admits the cited violation the Tribal Court shall 
proceed with a disposition that may as provided by this Section. 
 
(e) 
 If the cited party denies the cited violation the Tribal Court shall set the matter 
for an adjudicatory hearing without unnecessary delay. 
 
(f) 
 At the adjudicatory hearing the parties shall be allowed to present their cases. 
The Colony shall be represented by the Tribal Prosecutor and has the burden of 
proof by a preponderance of the evidence. The federal rules of evidence shall not 
apply. 

 3 
 
(g) 
At the adjudicatory hearing the tribal Court shall, based on the evidence 
presented, decide whether or not the Colony had proven the cited violation by a 
preponderance of the evidence and enter an appropriate disposition. 
 
(h) 
Any person found to have committed a civil offense under this Section may be 
sentenced to one or more of the following penalties for each offense found to have 
been committed: 
(1) 
A fine in the amount not to exceed the maximum permitted fine for 
the offense; 
(2) 
Restitution to any person or the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony for any 
losses or damages that resulted from the offense committed; 
(3) 
Prohibition from entering the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony; 
(4) 
 Forfeiture of any property subject to forfeiture under Title 4, Section 1-
108. (Amended by Resolution No. 2017-RS-35, 05/17/17)
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Civil Contempt. 
(a) 
Any person intentionally engaging in any of the following conduct may be held 
in civil contempt: 
(1) 
Disorderly, contemptuous, or insolent behavior committed during the 
sitting of Tribal Court, in its immediate view and presence, and directly 
tending to interrupt its proceedings or to impair the respect due its 
authority; 
(2) 
Breaching the peace by causing a disturbance directly tending to interrupt 
Tribal Court proceedings; 
(3) 
Disobeying or refusing any lawful process, disposition, order, order to 
appear or other mandate of the Tribal Court; 
(4) 
Refusing to be sworn as a witness in any Tribal Court proceeding or, after 
being sworn, unlawfully refusing to answer any legal and proper question 
 
(b) 
 Civil Contempt may be punishable by a fine of up to $1,000.00 per incident or by 
up to 30 days in jail. 
(1) 
It is not a required element that the act of civil contempt occurs in open 
court. 
(2) 
Acts which occur in open court require a warning by the Tribal Judge 
before a judgment of contempt may be entered. For contempt occurring in 
open court a person may be sentenced or sanctioned immediately. 
Contempt not occurring in open court must be set for a hearing before a 
judgment of Contempt may be issued. (Enacted by Resolution No. 2017-RS-
35, 05/17/17)
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

heading: Limitations of Prosecution Based on Same Transaction. Unless requested
text:
by the defendant or unless justice so requires, a defendant shall not be subject to separate trials in 
Tribal Court for multiple offenses based on the same conduct, if such offenses are known to the 
Tribal Prosecutor, or other counsel, at the time the first trial commences, and such offenses are 
within the jurisdiction of the Tribal Court.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Time limitations for Prosecution. 
 
(a) 
Unless otherwise specified in a particular section of this Code, prosecution for 
any offense shall be commenced within two years after the alleged offense is 
committed. 
 
(b) 
Prosecution for the offenses of Theft, Burglary, Forgery, Arson, Reckless Burning 
or Sexual Assault must be commenced within three years after the alleged offense 
is committed. 
 
(c) 
 Prosecution for the offense of Sexual Abuse of a Child must be commenced 
before the alleged victim of the sexual abuse is: 
(1) 
Twenty-one years old if he discovers or reasonably should have 
discovered that he was a victim of the sexual abuse by the date on which 
he reaches that age; or 
(2) 
Twenty-eight years old if he does not discover and reasonably should not 
have discovered that he was a victim of the sexual abuse by the date on 
which he reaches 21 years of age. 
 
(d) 
If any offense is committed in a secret manner, prosecution of the offense shall be 
commenced within the prescribed period of limitation and after the discovery of 
the offense. 
 
(e) 
For purposes of determining commencement of prosecution of offenses 
committed in a secret manner, discovery of an offense occurs when any person, 
including the victim, but other than the wrongdoer or someone acting in 
agreement with the wrongdoer, has knowledge of the ac and is criminal nature, 
unless the person with knowledge. 
(1) 
Fails to report out of fear induced by threats made by the wrongdoer or by 
anyone acting in agreement with the wrongdoer; or 

 10 
 
(2) 
Is a victim under 18 years of age and fails to report because of threats or 
coercive tactics of the perpetrator or from the child’s personal fear of not 
being believed. 
 
(f) 
An offense is committed either when the elements of the offense occur, or, when 
the offense is based upon a continuing course of conduct, at the time the course of 
conduct was terminated. Time starts to run on the day after the offense is 
discovered. 
 
(g) 
A prosecution is commenced when either a citation or a complaint is filed.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
When time limitations for prosecution suspended, extended, or removed. 
 
(a) 
The period of limitation is suspended under the following conditions: 
(1) 
During any period in which the offender is not usually and publicly 
residing with the Colony or is beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribal Court; 
(2) 
During any period in which the offender is a public officer and the offense 
charged is theft of public funds while in public office; 
(3) 
During a prosecution pending against one offender for the same conduct 
even if the prosecution is dismissed; or 
(4) 
During any period in which an alleged victim of sexual assault is insane, 
mentally retarded, mentally incompetent or in a medically comatose or 
vegetative state. 
 
(b) 
If, at any time during the prescribed period of limitation, an alleged victim of 
Attempted Homicide, Kidnapping. Aggravated Kidnapping, Unlawful Restraint 
or False Imprisonment, or person authorized to act on behalf of such an alleged 
victim, files with a law enforcement officer a written report concerning the 
offense, the prescribed period of limitation is extended for five years. 
 
(c) 
If, at any time during the prescribed period of limitation, an alleged victim of 
sexual assault, or a person authorized to act on behalf of an alleged victim of 
sexual assault, files with a law enforcement officer a written report concerning the 
sexual assault, the period of limitation is removed and there is no limitation of 
time within which a prosecution of sexual assault must be commenced.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Classification of Offenses and Penalties. 
 
(a) 
The offenses shall be designated as a Class A, B, C, D or E Offenses. 
(1) 
Class C: The Tribal Court may impose a sentence on a convicted person 
which may include, but is not limited to, an incarceration period not to 
exceed one (1) year and/or a fine not to exceed $5,000, and /or community 
service hours not to exceed 1000 hours. 

 11 
 
(2) 
Class B: The Tribal Court may impose a sentence on a convicted person 
which may include, but is not limited to, an incarceration period not to 
exceed 270 days and/or a fine not to exceed $1000 and/or community 
service hours not to exceed 600 hours. 
(3) 
Class A: The tribal Court may impose a sentence on a convicted person 
which may include, but is not limited to, an incarceration period not to 
exceed 180 days and/or a fine not to exceed $500 and /or community 
service hours not to exceed 300 hours. 
(4) 
Class D: $25.00 fine. 
(5) 
Class E: $50.00 fine. 
 
(b) 
All fines listed above may be imposed in addition to any assessment of costs or 
other civil penalties, and in addition to any amounts ordered paid as restitution 
. 
(c) 
Any person adjudged guilty of an offense under this Title shall be sentenced in 
accordance with this section, unless otherwise specified by a particular code 
provision.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

heading: Additional penalty for offenses committed by adults with assistance of a
text:
child. 
 
(a) 
An adult who commits an offense as set forth in this Title with assistance of a 
child shall be subject to incarceration for an additional term equal to the term of 
incarceration or penalty as prescribed by the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony Law and 
Order Code for the offense, except that no sentence for an offense shall exceed 
the maximum sentence permitted by the Indian Civil Rights Act. 
 
(b) 
This section does not create a separate offense, but provides an additional Penalty 
for the primary offense, the imposition of which penalty is contingent upon the 
finding of the prescribed fact. 
 
Part 3. Violent offender Registration.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Registration of violent offenders. 
 
(a) 
All persons who come on to the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony to visit, work or 
reside, who have been convicted of any of the offenses listed in subsection (b) 
below, must register with the Tribal Police and be fingerprinted within 48 hours 
of arriving on the Colony. All persons who register shall notify the police of any 
change of address within 72 hours after changing addresses. 
 
(b) 
Offenders who have been convicted of at least one of the following are required to 
register pursuant to this Part: 

 12 
 
(1)
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Record of registration. 
 
(a) 
The record of offender registration must include: 
(1) 
The name of the offender and all aliases that he has used; 
(2) 
A complete physical description of the offender, including scars, tattoos, 
birthmarks, and piercings, a current photograph of the offender, and 
fingerprints; 
(3) 
Date of birth and social security number; 
(4) 
The identification number from a driver’s license or identification card 
issued to the offender; 
(5) 
Information regarding the residence of the offender, including: 
(i) 
The current address at which the offender lives; 
(ii) 
The length of time he has resided at that address and the length of 
time he expects to remain there; 
(iii) 
The address or location of any other place where he expects to 
reside in the future and the length of time he expects to reside 
there, and (d) the length of time he expects to be on the Colony; 
(6) 
Name, address and phone number of his employer; 
(7) 
License numbers and descriptions of all motor vehicles registered to or 
frequently driven by the offender; 
(8) 
The name of the court where he was convicted and the name and address 
of his probation or parole officer, if any; 
(9) 
The name of the penal institution where he was omitted; 
(10) 
The specific location where the offense was committed; 
(11) 
The age, gender, race and general physical description of his victim; 
(12) 
The method of operation that was used to commit the offense, including, 
but not limited to: 
(i) 
Specific acts committed against the victim; 

 13 
 
(ii) 
The method of obtaining access to the victim, such as use of 
enticements, threats, forced entry or violence against the victim; 
(iii) 
The type of injuries inflicted on the victim; 
(iv) 
The types of instruments, weapons or objects used, the type of 
property taken; or 
(v) 
Any other distinctive characteristic of the behavior or personality 
of the offender. (Amended by Resolution 2013-RS-54, 07/17/13)
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

heading: Prohibited disclosure of information. Information that is disclosed pursuant
text:
to the provisions of this Chapter must not reveal the name of the victim of an offense, without 
the victim’s consent.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Failure to register or providing false information. 
 
(a) 
Any violent offender who fails to register as required by this chapter within 48 
hours after the conviction or after arriving on the Colony for the purpose of 
residing, employment, or setting up a temporary domicile for thirty days or more, 
is guilty of a Class B offense. 
 
(b) 
Any offender who provides false information to the Tribal police Department, 
when registering as a violent offender pursuant to this chapter, is guilty of a Class 
B offense. (Amended by Resolution 2013-RS 54, 07/17/13) 
 
CHAPTER 2- REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE 
 
Part 1. Requisite Intent to Commit an Offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS

text:
Required Mental State. 
(a) 
A person is not guilty of an offense unless he acted intentionally, knowingly, or 
negligently, as the law may require, with respect to each element of the offense, 
or unless the person’s acts constitute an offense involving strict liability. 
 
(b) 
If negligence is the mental state specified in the definition of an offense, a person 
may also be convicted if he acts intentionally or knowingly. If knowingly is the 

 14 
 
mental state specified in the definition of an offense, a person may also be 
convicted if he acts intentionally.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

heading: Strict Liability. A person may be guilty of an offense without having a
text:
requisite mental state, if the Code provision defining the offense indicates there is no required 
mental state, as provided by § 4-2-101. 
 
Part 2. Other Principles of Liability.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

text:
Ignorance or mistake of fact. Ignorance or mistake as to a matter of fact is a 
defense only if the ignorance or mistake negates a specific mental state required for the offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

heading: Ignorance or mistake of law. A belief that conduct does not legally
text:
constitute an offense is not a defense unless the law defining the offense has not been published 
or reasonably made available prior to the defendant’s conduct.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

heading: Liability for acts of corporations or unincorporated associations. A person
text:
is legally responsible for any conduct he performs or causes to be performed in the name of a 
corporation or unincorporated association or on its behalf, to the same extent as if it were 
performed in his own name or behalf.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

text:
Conduct and result. 
 
(a) 
Conduct is the cause of result if: 
(1) 
Without the conduct the result would not have occurred; and 
(2) 
Any additional causal requirements imposed by the specific code are not 
satisfied. 
 
(b) 
If intentionally or knowingly causing a result is an element of an offense and the 
result is not within the contemplation or intent of the defendant, either element 
can nevertheless be established if: 
(1) 
The final result differs from the intended result only in the respect that a 
different person or different property is affected or that the injury or harm 
caused is less than originally intended; or 
(2) 
The result involves the same kind of harm or injury as intended, but the 
precise harm or injury is different, or occurred in a different way, unless 
the actual result is too remote or accidental to have a bearing on the 
defendant’s liability or on the gravity of the offense. 
 

 15 
 
(c) 
If negligently causing a particular result is an element of an offense and the 
defendant is not aware or should not have been aware of the probable result, 
negligence can nevertheless be established if: 
(1) 
The actual result differs from the probable result only in the respect that a 
different person or different property is affected or that the actual injury or 
harm is less; or 
(2) 
The actual result involves the same kind of injury or harm as the probable 
result, unless the actual result is too remote or accidental to have a bearing 
on the defendant’s liability or on the gravity of the offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

text:
Voluntary Act. 
 
(a) 
A person is not guilty of an offense unless his guilt is based on a willful and 
voluntary act, or omission to perform an act, of which he is physically capable. 
 
(b) 
A reflex or convulsion, a bodily movement during unconsciousness or sleep, 
conduct during hypnosis, or a bodily movement that is otherwise not the product 
of the effort or determination of the person, are not voluntary acts within the 
meaning of this section. 
 
(c) 
Guilt may not be based on an omission to act unless a duty to perform the omitted 
act is specifically imposed by the Code.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

text:
Accountability. 
 
(a) 
A person is legally accountable for the conduct of another when: 
(1) 
Having a mental state described by the section defining the offense, the 
person causes another to perform the conduct, regardless of the legal 
capacity or mental state of the other person; 
(2) 
The section defining the offense makes the person accountable; 
(3) 
Either before or during the commission of an offense, with the purpose to 
promote or facilitate such commission, the person solicits, aids, abets, 
agrees, or attempts to aid such other person in the planning or commission 
of the offense. 
 
(b) 
However, a person is not accountable if: 
(1) 
A person is a victim of the offense committed; or 
(2) 
Before the commission of the offense the person terminates his efforts to 
promote or facilitate the commission of the offense and takes steps to 
negate the effect or otherwise prevent the commission of the offense. 
 
(c) 
 Person may be legally accountable for an offense which exceeds the offense 
which he was promoting or facilitating, if the commission of the excessive 

 16 
 
offense was reasonably foreseeable as a by-product of the planned offense, i.e., 
the shooting of a security guard during a person’s commission of the act of 
stealing property. 
 
(d) 
A person may be convicted of an offense on proof of the commission of an 
offense and his participation, even though the person who is claimed to have 
committed the offense has not been prosecuted for, or convicted of, the same or 
any other offense. 
 
(e) 
A person may not be found guilty of an offense on the testimony of one 
responsible or legally accountable for the same offense unless hat testimony is 
corroborated by other evidence that in itself, and without the aid to the testimony 
of the one responsible or legally accountable for the same offense, tends to 
connect the person with the commission of the offense. 
 
CHAPTER 3- AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES 
 
Part 1. Preliminary Provisions.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 2 REQUIREMENT TO COMMIT AN OFFENSE

text:
Consent. 
 
(a) 
Consent of the victim to conduct constituting an offense or to the result thereof, is 
a defense if such consent negates an element of the offense. 
 
(b) 
Consent is not a defense if the bodily harm consented to or threatened by the 
offense is serious. Consent that is given by a person who, by reason of youth, 
mental disease or defect, or intoxication, is unable to make a reasonable judgment 
is not valid.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

heading: Compulsion. A person is not guilty of an offense by reason of conduct which
text:
he performs under the compulsion or threat of imminent infliction of death or serious bodily 
harm if he reasonably believes that death or serious bodily harm will be inflicted upon him if he 
does not perform such conduct.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

heading: Duress. It is a defense that a person who engaged in the conduct constituting
text:
an offense did so under threat of force, fear, or coercion to himself or a family member, so long 
as the offense is not one which is likely to cause serious property damage or bodily harm.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

heading: Justification. Justification is a defense when the person’s conduct is
text:
reasonable and in fulfillment of his duties as a Tribal officer or employee, or is in reasonable 
discipline of a minor by a parent, guardian, teacher or other person in the position of parent.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

text:
Insanity Defense. 
 
(a) 
Affirmative defense. It is an affirmative defense to a prosecution under any 
provision of Title IV – Criminal Offenses, of the Law and Order Code that, at the 
time of the commission of the acts constituting the offense, the defendant, as a 
result of a severe mental disease or defect, was unable to appreciate the nature and 
quality or the wrongfulness of his acts. Mental disease or defect does not 
otherwise constitute a defense. 
 
(b) 
Burden of proof. The defendant has the burden of proving the defense of 
insanity by clear and convincing evidence. 
 
(c) 
If a person is found not guilty pursuant to this section, the Tribal Court shall 
follow the procedures in Title III, Chapter 10, Section 3-1-009.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

text:
Use of force in defense of a person. 
 
(a) 
A person is justified in using force, or threatening to use force, against another 
person when, and to the extent that he reasonably believes that, such force is 
necessary to defend himself or another against the imminent use of unlawful 
force. 
 
(b) 
A person is justified in the use of force likely to cause death or serious bodily 
harm only if he reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent 
imminent death or serious bodily harm to himself or another. 
 
(c) 
A person is not justified in using force under the above sections if he was the 
aggressor, or was engaged in combat by consent, unless he has withdrawn from 
the encounter and effectively communicated his withdrawal to the other person. 
 
(d) 
A person is not justified in using force under the above sections if he initially 
provoked the use of force upon himself with the intent to use such force as an 
excuse to inflict harm upon another. 
 
(e) 
A person is not justified in using deadly force if the other person is fleeing or has 
committed an offense against property only. Only such force as is necessary to 
subdue the defendant may be used if he is fleeing or after the commission of an 
offense against property. 
 

 18
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

text:
Use of Force in defense of occupied structure. 
 
(a) 
A person is justified in using force against another person when and to the extent 
necessary to prevent or terminate another person’s unlawful entry into, or attack 
upon, an occupied structure. 
 
(b) 
A person may use of force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm only if the 
entry is made or attempted in a violent manner, or it reasonably appears that there 
may be violence committed against any person in the occupied structure.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

text:
Use of force in defense of property. 
 
(a) 
A person is justified in using force, other than deadly force, when and to the 
extent he reasonably believes such force is necessary, to prevent or terminate 
criminal interference with either real property (other than an occupied structure) 
or personal property lawfully in his possession or in his immediate family’s 
possession, or property he has a duty to protect. 
 
(b) 
A person justified in the use of force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm 
only if he reasonably believes such force is necessary to prevent the commission 
of any Class C offense which involves the use, or threat of use of, physical force 
or violence against any person. 
 
CHAPTER 4 – INCHOATE (PREPARATORY) OFFENSES 
 
Part 1. Enumeration of Offenses and Extent of Liability.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 3 AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES

text:
Solicitation. 
 
(a) 
It shall be unlawful to entice, advise, incite, order or otherwise encourage another 
to commit an offense punishable under the laws of the jurisdiction under this 
code. 
 
(b) 
Violation of this section is a Class A offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 4 INCHOATE (PREPARATORY) OFFENSES

text:
Conspiracy. 
 
(a) 
If two or more people plan, or agree or consent to engage in, conduct constituting 
an offense and any one of them commits an overt act toward the commission of 
the agreed offense, each is guilty of the offense of conspiracy. 
 

 19 
 
(b) 
One can be guilty of conspiracy to commit an offense if the offense was 
reasonably foreseeable as an outcome of the offense to which he conspired to 
commit. 
 
(c) 
It shall be a defense to conspiracy that, before the commission of the offense, the 
person charged made an effort to withdraw from the conspiracy and took steps to 
negate the effect or otherwise prevent the commission of the offense. 
 
(d) 
Conspiracy to commit an offense is the same classification of offense as the 
offense that is the subject of the conspiracy, or the offense that was reasonably 
foreseeable and that resulted from the conspiracy.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 4 INCHOATE (PREPARATORY) OFFENSES

heading: Attempt
text:
(a) 
A person is guilty of an attempt to commit an offense, if, acting with the same 
mental state otherwise required for the commission of the offense, he engages in 
conduct constituting a substantial step toward commission of the offense, without 
completion of the offense attempted. 
 
(b) 
It is not a defense to the attempted commission of an offense that the 
consummation of the offense was impossible, as long as the offense could have 
been committed had the circumstances been as the person believed them to be. 
 
(c) 
Attempt is the same class of offense as the offense attempted. 
 
CHAPTER 5 – OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON 
 
Part 1. Preliminary Provisions
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 4 INCHOATE (PREPARATORY) OFFENSES

text:
Definitions. 
 
(a) 
‘Bodily harm or injury” means physical pain, illness, or an impairment of physical 
condition, and includes mental illness or impairment. 
 
(b) 
“Serious bodily harm or injury” means bodily harm or injury that: 
(1) 
Creates a substantial risk of death; 
(2) 
Causes serious permanent disfigurement or protracted loss or impairment 
of the function or process of a bodily member or organ; or 
(3) 
At the time of injury, can reasonably be expected to result in serious 
permanent disfigurement or protracted loss or impairment of the function 
or process of a bodily member or organ; or 
(4) 
Causes serious mental illness or impairment. 
 

 20 
 
Part 2. Homicide.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Homicide. 
 
(a) 
A person commits the offense of homicide by intentionally, knowingly or 
negligently causing the death of another human being. 
 
(b) 
Homicide as a Class C offense. If the offense is found to have been committed 
intentionally or knowingly, a conviction shall require the imposition of the 
maximum penalty for a Class C offense, both fine and jail, with no possibility of 
parole.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Aiding or soliciting suicide. 
 
(a) 
A person commits the offense of aiding or soliciting suicide by intentionally 
advising, encouraging or assisting another in taking his own life. 
 
(b) 
The fact that death did not result is not a defense. 
 
(c) 
Aiding or soliciting suicide is a Class B Offense. 
 
Part 3. Assault and Related Offenses.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Assault. 
 
(a) 
As used in this section, “assault” means intentionally placing another person in 
reasonable apprehension of immediate bodily harm. 
 
(b) 
A person convicted of an assault shall be punished: 
(1) 
If paragraph (3) or (4) of this subsection does not apply to the 
circumstances of the crime and the assault is not made with the use of a 
deadly weapon, or the present ability to use a deadly weapon, for a Class 
A offense. 
(2) 
If the assault is made with the use of the deadly weapon, or the present 
ability to use a deadly weapon, for a Class C offense. 
(3) 
If paragraph (4) of this subsection does not apply to the circumstances of 
the crime and if the assault is committed upon a law enforcement officer 
who is performing his duty and the person is charged knew or should have 
known that the victim was a law enforcement officer, for a Class B 
offense, unless the assault is made with the use of a deadly weapon, or the 
present ability to use a deadly weapon, then for a Class C offense. 
(4) 
If the assault is committed upon a law enforcement officer who is 
performing his duty, by a probationer, a prisoner who is in lawful custody 

 21 
 
or confinement or a parolee, and the probationer, prisoner or parolee 
charged knew or should have known that the victim was a law 
enforcement officer, then for a Class C offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Battery. 
 
(a) 
A person commits the offense of battery by intentionally causing harmful or 
offensive contact upon the person of another without that person’s consent. 
 
(b) 
Battery is a Class B offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Aggravated Battery. 
 
(a) 
A person commits the offense of Aggravated Battery by: 
(1) 
Intentionally causing serious bodily harm to another; 
(2) 
Intentionally causing bodily harm with a weapon to another; or 
(3) 
Knowingly causing serious bodily injury to another under circumstances 
manifesting indifference to the value of human life. 
(4) 
Battery upon a law enforcement officer. 
 
(b) 
Aggravated Battery is a Class C offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Making a violent threat. 
 
(a) 
Any person who intentionally makes a threat of physical violence to another, 
intending to cause such other person to be in fear for the safety of himself or of 
his family, is guilty of the offense of Making a violent Threat. Having the present 
ability to carry out the threat is not an element of the offense. 
 
(b) 
Making a Violent Threat is a Class A offense.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Harassment. 
 
(a) 
A person commits the crime of harassment by intentionally and without lawful 
authority: 
(1) 
Threatening to cause immediate or future bodily injury to the person 
threatened or to any other person; or 
(2) 
Threatening to cause physical damage to the property of another person; 
or 
(3) 
Threatening to subject the person threatened or any other person to 
confinement or restraint; or 
(4) 
Confronting or verbally abusing another, in person, in writing or by 
telephone; or 

 22 
 
(5) 
Threatening to do any act which is intended to substantially harm the 
person threatened or any other person with respect to his physical or 
mental health or safety; or 
(6) 
Making a telephone call with intent to annoy another or addressing any 
obscene language, representation or suggestion to or about any person 
receiving such call or addressing to such other person any threat to inflict 
injury to the person or property of the person addressed or any member of 
his family; and 
 
(b) 
The person, by words or conduct, places the person receiving the threat in 
reasonable fear that the threat will be carried out. 
 
(c) 
A person who is guilty of harassment: 
(1) 
For the first offense, is guilty of a Class B offense. 
(2) 
For the second or any subsequent offense, is guilty of a Class C offense. 
 
(d) 
Harassment shall be deemed to have been committed where the conduct occurred 
or where the person who was affected by the conduct was located at the time that 
the conduct occurred, and may be prosecuted at either place. 
 
(e) 
The penalties provided in this section do not preclude the victim from seeking any 
other legal remedy available.
heading_path: Title IV CRIMINAL OFFENSES > Chapter 5 OFFENSES AGAINST THE PERSON

text:
Stalking and Aggravated Stalking: penalties. 
 
(a) 
A person, other than a person in one of the relationships covered by the Family
